---
title: "Dai"
subtitle: "China"
region: "East Asia"
tags: [ethnography, east-asia]
---

## Overview

The Dai are several Tai-speaking peoples of southern Yunnan, concentrated in the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture and the Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, and counted by the People's Republic of China as one of its 56 officially recognized ethnic groups. "Dai" is a Han Chinese umbrella term with no equivalent in the Tai languages themselves, which have only broader words for Tai people in general; the groups it covers — speakers of *Tai Lü* (Sipsongpanna Dai) and *Tai Nüa* (Dehong Dai), of *Tai Dam* and of *Tai Ya* — are distinct culturally and linguistically. Figures compiled for Yunnan give roughly 400,000 speakers each for Tai Lü and Tai Nüa, about 40,000 for Tai Rui and about 20,000 for the Tianxin variety. In folk-culture terms the Dai matter as one of the few peoples native to China who practise Theravada Buddhism, with their own script, calendar and monastic literacy, and as cotton-and-silk weavers whose patterned cloth reached European museums in the twentieth century.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources document the Dai mainly through woven and embroidered cloth. Wikipedia names weaving first among Dai handicrafts, alongside oil-pressing, winemaking and bamboo work; the museum records give the fabrics themselves, without vernacular names for the techniques.

**Supplementary-weft cloth** — A fabric collected in 1949 at the Jinghong market in Xishuangbanna by Acher Eskenasy and L. van Bussel, and catalogued by the National Museum of World Cultures Foundation simply as untreated cloth woven with supplementary wefts: the pattern is carried by extra weft floats rather than printed or applied.

**Indigo patterned lengths** — Lengths of indigo cotton cloth with multi-coloured patterning and fringes worked at both ends, held by the British Museum.

**Patterned bedding cloth** — Cotton bedsheets and bed blankets in patterned weave, some fringed at one end only, together with a long narrow patterned mattress-cover; the same weaving repertoire serves the household as well as dress.

**Embroidered cloth** — A worked textile of cotton ground and cotton thread, and a two-part belt combining cotton and silk, both embroidered.

**Plaited leaf containers** — A lidded box of leaf strips in plain weave, dyed black and red or left natural yellow, whose plaited surface deliberately imitates patterned cloth.

**Motif vocabulary.** Eight-sided star motifs; transverse stripes used as a ground for them; on the plaited box, a surface that mimics cotton textile with supplementary woven gold threads; fringed end-finishes on cloth lengths and blankets.

### Clothing & dress

Dai garments in the collections are women's tube skirts and a jacket. The skirts occur in three material combinations — plain cotton, cotton with silk, and silk alone — which suggests a graded wardrobe from workaday to best, though the catalogue entries do not say so outright; the jacket is cotton. Dress is completed by an embroidered belt made in two parts, of cotton and silk together, the most decorated single garment element recorded. The sources do not describe Dai head coverings, footwear, men's dress or any ceremonial costume distinct from daily wear, and give no vernacular garment names. One point of comparison is recorded: the small Muslim minority known as *Dai Paxi* or *Dai Hui*, descended from Hui merchants from Dali and elsewhere in Yunnan who settled in Xishuangbanna in the early nineteenth century and intermarried locally, wear dress similar to that of their Buddhist neighbours and share their language, customs, rituals and diet — their material culture is described as identical.

### Architecture

Dai villages stand on bamboo plains near rivers or streams. Houses are usually raised on stilts, and some are square in plan. A few are two-storeyed, the upper floor given over to living space and the lower to storage; that lower level is sometimes left without walls altogether, an open undercroft beneath the dwelling. The religious landscape of the village is equally built: until very recently every Dai village had at least one Buddhist temple, and larger villages two to five, these temples also serving as schools where boys sent as novices learned to read and write. Many were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution. Of the older monumental architecture, the sources record only that the twelfth-century Jinghong Golden Hall Kingdom had its capital at Jinghong, and that under the Ming the manorial lords of the region maintained their own armies, prisons and courts. No decorative scheme, roof type or construction detail beyond stilts and bamboo is described.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources name no Dai ceramic or metalworking tradition. What they do document is plant-fibre craft: bamboo work listed among the developed Dai handicrafts, a lidded box plaited from dyed leaf strips, and a model flag of woven and dyed vegetable fibre catalogued as religious or ritual equipment. Bamboo is also a cooking vessel — the fragrant bamboo tube in which glutinous rice is baked. Oil-pressing and winemaking round out the handicraft economy, which since the 1980s has sat alongside tourism revenue in Xishuangbanna following the opening of airports at Jinghong and Mangshi.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Dai jewelry, tattooing or hair practices.

## Music & performance

The sources used — the Wikipedia articles and the museum catalogue records of the objects shown here — contain no account of Dai instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe any Dai dance or dramatic tradition; the only performance-like practice they record is the mutual pouring of water by young men and women at the New Year, described under Festivals below.

## Festivals & rituals

Dai festivals are mostly religious, and three are named. The **door closing festival** falls on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the Dai calendar, the middle of July in the Gregorian calendar; the **door opening festival** on the fifteenth day of the twelfth Dai month, the middle of October. On both days everyone goes to the Buddhist temple for ritual observance, offering food, flowers and coins to the Buddha. The three months between them are the "closed" season, the most intensely religious part of the year.

The **Water Splashing Festival** is the Dai New Year — glossed as the New Year of June, since it falls in the late sixth or early seventh month of the Dai calendar, the middle of April in the Gregorian calendar, about ten days after Qingming. It is called the most beautiful day of the year and usually lasts three days. At first light villagers go to the temple to wash the figure of the Buddha; after the temple ceremony young men and women pour water over one another, and then move through the settlement in groups sprinkling passers-by as a blessing. The equivalent festival among related Tai-speaking peoples is Songkran.

The central life-cycle rite recorded is monastic: parents commonly sent sons between seven and eighteen to a monastery as novices, where they stayed three years or more learning to read, write and practise the faith before most returned to secular life. Marriage was historically contracted between families of similar social and economic standing, and polygamy was common among chieftains.

## Foodways

Rice is the staple; in the Dehong area it is mainly japonica rice. The best-known Dai snack is **bamboo rice**, glutinous rice packed into a fragrant bamboo tube, soaked in water for about fifteen minutes and then baked over a fire. **Pineapple purple rice** is a second well-known dish. Dai cooking is characterized as raw, fresh, sour and spicy, and the preferences are explained in the sources as dietary reasoning: sour food is held to brighten the eyes, aid digestion and relieve heat, sweet to lift fatigue, and spicy to sharpen the appetite. Sourness is reckoned the finest flavour, and most dishes and snacks are built around it — **sour bamboo shoots** and **sour pork** are the examples given. The subtropical setting supplies the rest of the larder: rice, coffee, rubber, tea, sugar and many kinds of fruit are grown, and winemaking is one of the household crafts. The *Dai Paxi* Muslim minority is recorded as keeping a diet similar to that of Buddhist Dai.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Dai have a substantial written and oral literature: historical documents, legends, stories, poetry, fables and children's stories are described as plentiful. Alongside them stands an astronomical literature — many books on calculating solar and lunar eclipses, most of them written in Dai script — and the Dai calendar itself, which begins in the year 638. The transmission mechanism is the village monastery: because boys were routinely sent to learn reading and writing there, literacy in Dai script among Dai men is reported today to exceed 80 percent. The sources name no single epic or storytelling genre, and do not describe proverb or riddle traditions.

## Language & religion

Dai peoples in China speak Southwestern Tai languages of the Tai–Kadai family: Tai Lü, Tai Nüa (also called Dehong Dai, and identified with Shan), Tai Dam, and Tai Ya or Tai Hongjin; four major varieties are usually distinguished, Tai Lü, Tai Nüa, Tai Rui and Tianxin, the last represented by the dialect of Tianxin in Wuding County. Two further written languages used by the Dai are Tày Pong and Tai Dam. Related Tai–Kadai languages are spoken from Assam to Hainan and Guizhou. The Dai are predominantly Theravada Buddhists, having converted during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries although Buddhism had been present in Yunnan since at least the seventh; earlier animism was not displaced, and belief in natural spirits continues within Dai Buddhism. A small minority are Muslim.

Dai material culture centers on woven and embroidered cloth, with patterned fabrics as the most documented tradition, alongside bamboo work, oil-pressing, and winemaking.

Dai weavers create patterned cloth using supplementary wefts, indigo patterning, and embroidery, with eight-sided star motifs and transverse stripes as common designs.

- **Plaited leaf containers** — Lidded boxes of leaf strips in plain weave, dyed black and red or left natural yellow, with surfaces that mimic patterned cloth.

### Clothing & dress

Dai dress consists of women's tube skirts and jackets in plain cotton, cotton with silk, or silk alone, completed by embroidered belts.

title: "Tai Nua"
subtitle: "China"
region: "East Asia"
tags: [ethnography, east-asia]
---

## Overview

The Tai Nua — also written Tai Nuea, Tai Neua, Tai Nüa or Dai Nua, and known as Dehong Dai or Chinese Shan — are one of the Tai peoples of Southeast Asia, concentrated in the borderlands where southwest China meets northeast Myanmar and spread onward into Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Their settlements follow the Shweli and Salween river valleys; in China most live in the Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture of western Yunnan, particularly around Mangshi, Ruili and Lianghe County, where the population is estimated at roughly 650,000 as of 2026, with a further 100,000–150,000 speakers in Myanmar's Northern Shan State towns of Muse, Namkham and Kutkai. Their language belongs to the Tai family, and they matter in folk-culture terms above all for possessing their own script, the Tai Le or Dehong Dai script, and for a body of festival practice, theatre and weaving distinct from that of the Tai Lue of Sipsongpanna to the south.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The catalogue records behind this gallery document two kinds of cloth, both woven rather than printed or embroidered.

**Shoulder cloth** — a narrow woven cloth patterned with red and blue supplementary weft yarns, which the cataloguer describes as carrying typical Tai geometric patterning. The supplementary-weft technique, in which extra coloured wefts float above a plain ground weave, is what produces the banded ornament.

**Offering cloth** — cotton cloths made for presentation, held in the collection as a pair. The records give the material and the purpose but no further detail of weave, dye or motif.

Beyond these, the sources used here do not describe a named repertoire of Tai Nua pattern traditions, and no motif names are recorded in them.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Tai Nua dress in any systematic way. From the collection records, the only garment or accessory documented besides the shoulder cloth is a hat made of straw. The shoulder cloth itself belongs to the shawl-and-wrap class of Tai dress, worn over the upper body rather than tailored, but the records do not say by whom, on what occasions, or how men's and women's wear differ. One dress-adjacent practice is documented in the festival material: at New Year, children present their elders with an offering of flowers when asking forgiveness, a gesture described in terms of the offering rather than of costume. For everyday versus ceremonial wardrobes, for head coverings other than the straw hat, and for belts and footwear, the sources consulted offer nothing.

### Architecture

The sources used for this profile do not cover Tai Nua house form, building materials, roof construction or architectural ornament. The only built structure they name is the Buddhist temple, which serves as the site of the final and largest day of the New Year festival, where monks give their blessing; nothing is said about its plan or decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Metalwork is represented in the collection by a **sword** made of metal and rattan — a blade with rattan used in its mounting or binding, the combination of worked metal with a plaited plant fibre being characteristic of Southeast Asian edged weapons. The same plant-fibre skill appears in the straw hat. Two festival object types are documented in the New Year material: the *Ki Tong Ja*, a swing used during the holiday, and the spinning tops played with alongside it; a straw effigy of a bull is built for the last day of the festival and burned. The sources used do not describe Tai Nua ceramics, lacquer, basketry beyond the hat, or household utensils.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used for this profile record no Tai Nua jewelry, silverwork, tattooing or hair practice.

## Music & performance

Music reaches the sources chiefly through the theatre. **Daiju** (傣剧), the Tai Nua and wider Dai dramatic form, combines Dai music and dance with narrative material, and it is the vehicle in which the group's melodic and choreographic repertoire is documented. It is most popular in the Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture and in neighbouring Baoshan, at the western edge of Yunnan along the Kachin and Shan State borders. Its music is syncretic by formation: when Dai performers and intellectuals built the genre in the late Qing period, they translated scripts out of Beijing opera, Sichuan opera and Dianju (滇剧, Yunnan opera) into the Dai language, and the resulting theatre blends those Han Chinese stage traditions — along with *piyingxi* (皮影戏), shadow puppet play — with Dai song and dance.

Broadcast is the other documented performance channel: Yunnan People's Radio Station transmits in Tai Nuea, which has official status in parts of Yunnan and appears on road and shop signs in Mangshi.

The festival calendar supplies the main secular performance occasions. The New Year week is given over to swinging on the *Ki Tong Ja*, spinning tops, and competitive games — *Toh Mark Khang* and the bean-bag tossing game *Peak Gon* — culminating in a temple gathering with the monks' blessing. The sources used do not name Tai Nua instruments or song genres individually.

## Dance & theatre

**Daiju** is the named dramatic tradition. It is classified in Chinese scholarship as a form of minority drama (*shaoshan minzu xiqu*, 少数民族戏曲) and takes its plots from long narrative poems and from folk tales, many of the latter drawn from Buddhist tradition. Its origin is precisely dated in the sources: during the reign of the Tongzhi Emperor (同治帝, r. 1861–1875), Shang He (尚贺), a resident of Yingjiang County (盈江县, then called Ganya, 干崖) in what is now Dehong Prefecture, worked from older Dai literature to compose the first Daiju play, *Xiang Meng* (相勐). The genre as a whole took shape in the late Qing Dynasty out of the translation effort described above, so Daiju stands as a deliberately constructed theatre for Dai audiences rather than an inherited village form. The sources used do not name individual Tai Nua dances apart from the dance element within Daiju.

## Festivals & rituals

The documented centrepiece of the year is the New Year festival, *Jin Leun Sam*, which normally falls on the first day of the third month of the lunar calendar. It draws people living away from home back to their birthplaces, and the festivities can run for a week. During that week the swing *Ki Tong Ja* is set up, spinning tops are played, and the competitions *Toh Mark Khang* and *Peak Gon* (bean-bag tossing) are held. It is the occasion for *Su Ma*, when children ask their elders' forgiveness and present an offering of flowers. Households bake festival cakes and invite friends and relatives to a succession of special meals through the week, which peak on New Year's Day itself, *Meu Ho Leun Sam*. On the final day an effigy of a bull is made from straw and burned in a ceremony marking the departure of the old year, and the closing celebration is held at the temple with the blessing of the monks. The cotton offering cloths in this gallery belong to the same world of presented gifts, although the records do not tie them to a specific rite. The sources used do not describe Tai Nua birth, marriage or funeral observances.

## Foodways

Tai Nua festival food is rice food. Two named cakes are made for the New Year: *Khao Pook Nga*, sesame rice cakes, and *Kao Ke Mah*, rice ball cakes. These are not solitary dishes but the material of hospitality — friends and family are invited in for special meals repeatedly across the festival week, with the sequence culminating in the New Year's Day meal on *Meu Ho Leun Sam* before the celebration moves to the temple. Beyond these cakes and the pattern of invited meals, the sources used give no account of staple crops, cooking methods, everyday dishes, drink or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Tai Nua have their own literature, and two of its genres are named in the sources as the material Daiju playwrights drew on: long narrative poems and folk tales, the tales frequently Buddhist in origin. Older Dai literature was the direct source for *Xiang Meng*, the first Daiju play, composed in the 1860s or early 1870s from that written inheritance. Proverb collecting is the one documented modern preservation effort: in Thailand a collection of 108 Tai Nua proverbs has been published with translations into Thai and English. In China the situation is uneven — Tai Nuea has official standing in parts of Yunnan and is used in education and radio broadcasting, yet very little printed matter appears in the language.

## Language & religion

Tai Nuea belongs to the Tai language family and is closely related to Shan, of which it could be counted a dialect; it should not be confused with Tai Lü. Speakers mostly call themselves *Tai Le*, 'Upper Tai' or 'Northern Tai'; another autonym means 'Tai of the lower Hong River', the Hong being the Tai name for the Salween, and it is this phrase that gives the name Dehong. Zhou's classification divides the language into the Dehong dialect (332,000 speakers) and the Menggeng dialect (209,000), for a total of 541,000. The Laotian situation differs: Tai Nua speakers in Houaphanh Province use the Neua language, which has Northern Tai features, while the Yunnan variety is Southwestern Tai. The Tai Le script belongs to the Mon-Burmese family of writing systems, is closely related to the Ahom script and is thought to date to the 14th century; the reformed orthography was officially introduced in 1956, tone diacritics came in 1963, and in 1988 these were replaced by tone letters, giving a modern alphabet of 35 letters including five tone letters. On religion the sources are brief: Buddhist monks bless the close of the New Year festival at the temple, and Buddhist narrative supplies much of the folk-tale repertoire.

## Sources & further reading

- Schliesinger, Joachim. *Ethnic Groups of Laos Vol 3: Profile of Austro-Thai-Speaking Peoples.* BooksMango, 2015.
- Pierson, David E. *The Tai, an Ethnographic Survey: Understanding the People, Their Culture and Their Language.* University Press, 2007.
- Luo, Yongxian. *A Dictionary of Dehong, Southwest China.* Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, 1998.
- Zhou, Yaowen and Luo, Meizhen. *Dǎiyǔ fāngyán yánjiū: Yǔyīn, cíhuì, wénzì* (A study of Dai dialects: phonology, vocabulary, script). Beijing: Minzu chubanshe, 2001.
- Berlie, Jean A. *Neua (Na) in Yunnan (PRC) and the LPDR: A Minority and a "Non-Minority" in the Chinese and Lao Political Systems.* London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, 1993.
- Chantanaroj, Apiradee. *A Preliminary Sociolinguistic Survey of Selected Tai Nua Speech Varieties.* Master's thesis, Payap University, 2007.
- Wikipedia, "Tai Nua people": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Nua_people
- Wikipedia, "Tai Nua language": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Nua_language
- British Museum collection online (the sword, straw hat, shoulder cloth and offering cloths shown here): https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection

## Festivals & rituals

The New Year festival Jin Leun Sam, falling on the first day of the third lunar month, is the documented centrepiece of the Tai Nua year.

- **Jin Leun Sam** — The New Year festival normally falling on the first day of the third month of the lunar calendar, running for a week and drawing people back to their birthplaces.
- **Ki Tong Ja** — A swing set up during the New Year week for celebrations.
- **Su Ma** — The occasion when children ask their elders' forgiveness and present an offering of flowers.
- **Meu Ho Leun Sam** — New Year's Day itself, when the week's special meals culminate in a major feast.

## Foodways

Tai Nua festival food centers on rice cakes made for New Year, which anchor a pattern of hospitality and invited meals.

- **Khao Pook Nga** — Sesame rice cakes baked for the New Year festival.
- **Kao Ke Mah** — Rice ball cakes made for New Year celebrations as material for hospitality.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tai Nua have their own literature in long narrative poems and Buddhist-influenced folk tales that supply material for theatre.

- **Narrative poems** — Long narrative poems that served as source material for Daiju playwrights.
- **Folk tales** — Stories frequently drawn from Buddhist tradition, used as plot sources for Daiju theatre.
- **Tai Nua proverbs** — A collection of 108 Tai Nua proverbs has been published in Thailand with translations into Thai and English.

## Language & religion

Tai Nuea belongs to the Tai language family and has its own script, the Tai Le writing system, while Buddhism provides the religious framework and narrative tradition.

- **Tai Nuea language** (*Tai Nuea*) — A Tai language closely related to Shan, with speakers dividing into Dehong dialect (332,000 speakers) and Menggeng dialect (209,000).
- **Tai Le script** (*Tai Le*) — A Mon-Burmese writing system thought to date to the 14th century, with modern reforms introducing tone diacritics in 1963 and tone letters in 1988, creating an alphabet of 35 letters.

## Glossary

- *Daiju (傣剧)* — Tai Nua theatrical form blending Dai music, dance and narrative
- *Jin Leun Sam* — Tai Nua New Year festival on the first day of the third lunar month
- *Ki Tong Ja* — A swing used in New Year celebrations
- *Su Ma* — New Year occasion when children ask elders' forgiveness with flower offerings
- *Meu Ho Leun Sam* — New Year's Day, culminating day for festival meals
- *Khao Pook Nga* — Sesame rice cakes made for New Year
- *Kao Ke Mah* — Rice ball cakes made for New Year
- *Toh Mark Khang* — Competitive game played during New Year festival
- *Peak Gon* — Bean-bag tossing game played at New Year
- *Tai Nuea* — The Tai Nua language, closely related to Shan
- *Tai Le* — Tai Nua writing system of the Mon-Burmese family; also an autonym meaning Upper Tai
- *Dehong* — Autonomous Prefecture in western Yunnan where most Tai Nua in China live; means Tai of the lower Hong River
- *Xiang Meng (相勐)* — The first Daiju play, composed during the Tongzhi Emperor's reign

---
title: "Bouyei"
subtitle: "China"
region: "East Asia"
tags: [ethnography, east-asia]
---

## Overview

The Bouyei (*Buxqyaix*; Chinese 布依族; also spelled Puyi, Buyei, Buyi) are a Tai-speaking people of the plains of southern Guizhou in China, concentrated in the Qianxinan and Qiannan prefectures and present also in Yunnan, Sichuan and the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with newer communities in the coastal provinces of Zhejiang and Guangdong. The 2020 census recorded 3,576,752 Bouyei, making them the tenth largest of the 56 ethnic groups officially recognised by the People's Republic of China; some 3,000 more live in northern Vietnam, where the Bố Y are one of 54 recognised groups. Their language belongs to the Northern Tai group of the Tai–Kadai family. In folk-culture terms they are known regionally for their handicrafts and batik, and the objects this atlas shows are almost entirely women's and girls' dress.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Batik** — wax-resist patterning on cotton; the sources state that Bouyei batiks, together with their other handicrafts, are renowned throughout the region. The British Museum woman's jacket in this collection combines batik with embroidery and appliqué on a single cotton garment.

**Embroidery and appliqué on cotton and silk** — the dominant technique in the catalogued objects: a girl's apron and a woman's apron, a pair of apron-ties, a pair of tie-belts and a baby-carrier are all recorded as cotton (sometimes with silk) worked in embroidery, appliqué or both.

**Embroidered ribbons** — narrow cotton-and-silk bands made to be sewn onto clothing; three are held as separate catalogued objects, indicating that ornament was produced as stock and applied to garments afterwards rather than worked only in place.

**Striped and patterned cloth** — the woman's head cover is a length of striped, patterned and embroidered cotton, the one piece in the group whose pattern is described as woven rather than applied.

The sources name no motifs, so no motif vocabulary is given here.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document dress only through the catalogued objects, and these are all female garments and accessories. A woman's outfit is represented by a cotton jacket decorated with batik, embroidery and appliqué; cotton trousers; an embroidered apron of cotton and silk with a matching pair of embroidered, appliquéd apron-ties; and a pair of cotton-and-silk tie-belts, recorded as belts worn in pairs. The head is covered with a length of striped, patterned, embroidered cotton rather than a shaped hat. Footwear is represented by a single pair of straw sandals. A small girl's apron, appliquéd and embroidered in cotton and silk, shows the same construction as the adult garment at child scale, and an embroidered baby-carrier of cotton and probable silk extends the same decorative repertoire to infant care. The sources do not describe men's dress, nor do they distinguish ceremonial from everyday clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Bouyei house form, building materials or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources record no Bouyei pottery, woodwork or agricultural tools. The only everyday objects catalogued are a pair of straw sandals and the embroidered baby-carrier; the only metalwork is silver personal ornament, treated below. The wider economic picture the sources give is agricultural and commercial rather than artisanal: the Bouyei farm rice, millet, wheat, potatoes, maize, cocoa, tea and silk for consumption or sale, and have long acted as intermediate merchants in their region, now operating businesses at both small and large scale.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Silver is the documented material for Bouyei personal ornament. The collection holds a woman's silver bracelet and a woman's silver finger-ring, both catalogued simply by form and metal. The sources describe no other jewellery types and say nothing about tattooing, hair practices or other body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Bouyei instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Bouyei dance. They do record a related textual tradition: *Nuo* books and Nuo scripts, written in the ancient Bouyei script, have circulated among the Bouyei of the Libo region for more than a thousand years, praising goodness, condemning evil, advocating filiality and promoting truth, kindness and beauty, to the point of serving as a local code of conduct. The sources present these as scriptures and texts and do not say how, or whether, they were performed.

## Festivals & rituals

Two annual observances are documented. **Ox King's Day** (牛王节), on April 8, honours oxen and their contribution to agricultural work. **June 6** — the sixth day of the sixth lunar month — is the important traditional holiday for ancestral worship, and the sources give the myth attached to it: Pangu, having mastered rice farming after creating the world, married the daughter of the Dragon King, and from their union the Bouyei arose. Their son Xinheng (新横) disrespected his mother, who returned to heaven and would not come down again despite the pleas of husband and son; Pangu remarried and died on the sixth day of the sixth month. Xinheng's stepmother mistreated him and nearly killed him, but when he threatened to destroy her rice harvest she recognised her fault, made peace with him, and the two began paying their respects to Pangu on that date each year. Ritual practice is also attested in writing: the collected ancient-script manuscripts are mostly shamans' books of the Bouyei ancestors, used to select auspicious days, lucky numbers and directions and for divination. Alongside these traditions the Bouyei celebrate festivals derived from Han culture, which the sources mention without naming. The sources describe no birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources name no Bouyei dishes, cooking methods or ceremonial foods. They record only the crops grown: rice, millet, wheat, potatoes, maize, cocoa and tea, cultivated for consumption or for sale, with rice prominent enough to anchor both the Pangu origin myth and the quarrel that gave June 6 its meaning.

## Oral tradition & literature

The one named literary work is the epic poem ***Wang Yulian***, understood as a retelling of a Chinese story in the Bouyei language; hand copies of it remain popular in Zhexiang Township, Wangmo County, in the Qianxinan Bouyei and Miao Autonomous Prefecture. The Nuo books described above form the other body of traditional literature, with the shamans' divination manuscripts beside them. Mythology is represented by the Pangu and Dragon King's daughter narrative that accounts for Bouyei origins and for the June 6 observance. Documentation and standardisation have continued through the modern period: Yu Cuirong published an introduction to the language in 1980 and Wu Qilu a Bouyei–Chinese dictionary in 2002, while the survey work of Wu, Snyder and Liang (2007) remains the most comprehensive on Bouyei speech, and Edmondson and Gregerson (2001) documented the related varieties in Vietnam.

## Language & religion

Bouyei (*Haausqyaix*) is a Northern Tai language of the Tai–Kadai family with over 2.5 million native speakers, about 98% of them in China, and stands in a dialect continuum with Standard Zhuang. A 1950s government survey divided Guizhou Bouyei into Southern, Central and Western groups, the western dialects the least spoken and the most distinctive, some of them retaining aspirated stops uncommon in Northern Tai. Writing has three layers: an ancient script built from borrowed or imitated Chinese characters, similar to Sawndip, used for shamans' and Nuo manuscripts; a Latin alphabet based on the Longli County dialect, approved in 1956 and used from 1957 to 1960; and the current script, redesigned between 1981 and 1985 on Wangmo County speech and official since March 1985. Religious life combines ancestral worship and divination with Christianity: Catholicism entered Guizhou in 1714, missionaries devised a Latin-based Bouyei script for religious education around 1797–1800, the Diocese of Nanlong was established in 1879 at Nanlong (now Anlong County), and churches remain in Guizhou and Yunnan.

## Sources & further reading

- Yu, Cuirong (喻翠容), 布依语简志 [Introduction to the Buyi Language], Beijing: Publishing House of Minority Nationalities, 1980
- Wu, Qilu (吴启禄), 布依汉词典 [Bouyei–Chinese Dictionary], Beijing: Publishing House of Minority Nationalities, 2002 (ISBN 7-105-04965-0)
- Wu, Snyder & Liang (2007), the most comprehensive Bouyei dialect survey to date; Snyder (2008) on the three Guizhou dialect groups
- Edmondson & Gregerson (2001), on the Bouyei, Giáy and Bố Y varieties of northern Vietnam; Lò (2012) on the Pu Nả of Tam Đường District
- Wikipedia, "Bouyei people": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouyei_people
- Wikipedia, "Bouyei language": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouyei_language
- Ethnologue entry for Bouyei, and the ABVD Bouyei (Wangmo) word list
- British Museum online collection (the jacket, aprons, apron-ties, belts, head cover, trousers, sandals, baby-carrier, ribbons and silver ornaments shown here): https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element in the sources concerns the Bouyei.

---
title: "Bretons"
subtitle: "France"
region: "Europe"
tags: [ethnography, europe]
---

## Overview

The Bretons (*Bretoned* or *Vretoned* in Breton) are a Celtic people native to Brittany, the north-western peninsula of France. The demonym originally designated Brittonic speakers who emigrated from south-western Great Britain — particularly Cornwall and Devon — in waves from the 3rd to the 9th century, most heavily between 450 and 600, settling the western part of Armorica, which was subsequently named after them. Brittany's population was estimated at 4,365,500 in January 2007, a figure that appears to include the department of Loire-Atlantique, which the Vichy government separated from historical Brittany in 1941; France does not collect statistics on ethnicity, so the number of Bretons as such cannot be established. The traditional language, *Brezhoneg*, belongs to the Brittonic branch of Celtic, alongside Cornish and Welsh. Brittany has historically been counted as one of the six Celtic nations, and its festival, pilgrimage and music traditions remain among the most actively practised folk cultures in France.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources available for this profile — the Wikipedia article on the Bretons and the catalogue records of the Metropolitan Museum of Art objects shown here — describe Breton textiles only through the garments themselves, not through named weaving or embroidery traditions. What the catalogue records establish is a consistent 19th-century repertoire of wool garments worked with coloured wool thread, metal thread, glass beads and metal spangles or paillettes:

**Beaded and metal-thread woollens** — The Met's Breton holdings are jackets, vests, bodices and skirts of wool, decorated with wool thread, metal thread and glass beads; one 19th-century set comprises a matching jacket, bodice and skirt. Several late-19th-century jackets and vests use glass beads together with metal paillettes rather than metal thread.

**Silk-lined jackets and vests** — A separate group of 19th-century jackets and vests pairs wool with silk, without beadwork.

**Decorative ribbons** — Silk ribbons worked with metal spangles (19th century) and with metal (late 19th–early 20th century) form part of the same costume complex, entering the collection alongside the garments they trimmed.

No motif names appear in the sources, so no motif vocabulary is given here.

### Clothing & dress

The dress documented for the Bretons in these sources is the 19th- and early-20th-century costume represented by the Metropolitan Museum's objects. Women's dress is attested by bodices and skirts of wool worked in wool thread, metal thread and glass beads, assembled as matching ensembles with a jacket. Jackets and vests occur in both the beaded and metal-spangled form and in a plainer wool-and-silk form. Belts are represented by a single named object: a *gouriz* of leather and brass, dated about 1834. Silk ribbons with metal spangles trimmed these garments. Beyond this, the sources describe no head coverings, no footwear, and no distinction between everyday and ceremonial wear — though they do note that numerous people appear in traditional costume at the pardon of Locronan (*Lokorn*), so the costume complex remains in ceremonial use.

### Architecture

The sources used for this profile do not describe Breton house forms, building materials or vernacular ornament. The only built features they name are the shrines and parish churches of the seven founder saints — at Saint-Pol-de-Léon (*Kastell-Paol*), Tréguier (*Landreger*), Saint-Brieuc (*Sant-Brieg*), Saint-Malo (*Sant-Maloù*), Dol-de-Bretagne (*Dol*), Vannes (*Gwened*) and Quimper (*Kemper*) — which anchor the *Tro Breizh* pilgrimage, and the memorial at Saint-Columban in Carnac commemorating the Irish saint Columbanus.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources name no Breton ceramic or woodworking tradition. The one metalwork object they document is the *gouriz*, a leather belt with brass fittings dated about 1834, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Metal otherwise appears in these records as costume material rather than as objects in its own right: metal thread couched onto woollen jackets, bodices and skirts; metal paillettes sewn alongside glass beads on late-19th-century jackets and vests; and metal spangles on silk ribbons. Brittany's other widely recognised emblematic objects named in the sources are not household goods but heraldic and symbolic devices — the ermine of the Duchy's blazons and of the chivalric *L'Ordre de l'Hermine*, and the triskele, a Celtic symbol Bretons use to assert their Celtic descent.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used for this profile do not describe Breton jewelry, tattooing, henna or hair practices; the only body-worn metal they document is the brass of the *gouriz* belt and the metal thread, paillettes and spangles applied to garments and ribbons.

## Music & performance

Breton music divides into two main types: a choral a cappella tradition called *kan ha diskan*, and instrumental music. The characteristic traditional instruments are the *bombard*, similar to an oboe, and two kinds of bagpipe — the *veuze* and the *binioù kozh*. Diatonic accordion, clarinet and, less often, violin and hurdy-gurdy are also commonly found. The basic clarinet, called *treujenn-gaol*, had very nearly disappeared before regaining popularity in recent years. After the Second World War the Great Highland bagpipe and the *binioù bras* became commonplace through the *bagadoù*, Breton pipe bands, and in many settings displaced the *binioù kozh*.

The principal performance context is the *fest-noz*, a festival built around dancing. Although many of its dances are old, some reaching back to the Middle Ages, the *fest-noz* as an institution dates from the 1950s; UNESCO inscribed it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 5 December 2012. Festoù-noz are now also held well outside Brittany, carrying the regional repertoire with them — a Breton association in China organises a "Fest-noz de Pékin". Contemporary groups work in registers from rock and jazz (Red Cardell) through ethno-rock (Diwall, Skeduz) to punk, and some *fest-noz* bands, among them Strobinell, Sonerien Du, Les Baragouineurs and Plantec, use electronic keyboards and synthesisers.

## Dance & theatre

The best-known Breton dances are the *gavottes*, the *An Dro*, the *hanter dro* and the *plinn*. At a *fest-noz* most dancing is done in a chain or a circle, with participants linking little fingers; there are also couple dances and choreographed dances built from set sequences and figures. Processional movement is central to Breton religious practice as well: the pardon of Locronan includes a *troménie*, a procession twelve kilometres long, walked by large numbers of people in traditional costume. The sources describe no Breton dramatic or theatrical tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The Breton festival year is organised around *pardons*, each the feast day of a parish's patron saint. A pardon typically opens with a procession, followed by mass in the saint's honour, and is frequently accompanied by a small village fair. The three most celebrated are **Sainte-Anne d'Auray** (*Santez-Anna-Wened*), **Tréguier** (*Landreger*) in honour of St Yves, and **Locronan** (*Lokorn*) in honour of St Ronan, the last with its twelve-kilometre *troménie*.

The major pilgrimage is the *Tro Breizh*, the "tour of Brittany", in which pilgrims walk from the grave of one of the Seven Founder Saints to the next; today the circuit is usually completed over several years. In 2002 the *Tro Breizh* included a pilgrimage to Wales, symbolically reversing the journey made by the Welshmen Paul Aurelian, Brioc and Samson. Breton religious tradition holds that anyone who fails to make the pilgrimage once in life must make it after death, advancing only the length of their coffin every seven years. Attendance at Sunday mass fell through the 1970s and 1980s, but pilgrimage has revived.

The "national day" falls on 1 August, the Feast of Saint Erwann (Saint Yves); the largest Breton national event, the *Gouel Breizh*, takes place each year in the week of 19 May, the day Saint Yves died. The sources used here do not describe Breton birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral rites.

## Foodways

Breton cooking draws much from the wider French culinary tradition, with a set of local specialities the sources name directly. *Krampouezh* — crêpes or galettes — are thin pancakes made from either wheat or buckwheat flour, usually eaten as a main course rather than as a sweet. *Kouign-amann* is a butter pastry. *Fars forn*, also called *far breton*, is a sweet suet pudding with prunes. *Caramel au beurre salé*, salted butter caramel, rounds out the sweet repertoire. Three drinks belong to the same list: *sistr*, cider; *lambig*, an apple eau de vie; and *chouchenn*, a Breton mead. Pardons are accompanied by village fairs, and the *fest-noz* is a festival in its own right, but the sources do not specify which foods belong to which occasion, nor do they record dietary rules or a tea or coffee tradition.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources name no Breton epic or folktale cycle, but they do identify the central figure of Breton folk belief: the *Ankou*, the "Reaper of Death", described as the most powerful folk figure surviving from pre-Christian tradition in Brittany. Alongside it stands the body of legend around the seven founder-saints of Brittany and the numerous records of Celtic Christian missionaries migrating from Britain during the second wave of settlement — a hagiographic tradition so pervasive that, as in Cornwall, many Breton towns are named after these early saints. Written Breton culture is sustained today by a periodical press: *Al Lanv*, published in Quimper, along with *Al Liamm*, *Louarnig-Rouzig* and *Bremañ*. Breton-language broadcasting includes Arvorig FM, France Bleu Armorique, France Bleu Breizh-Izel, Radio Bro Gwened, Radio Kerne and Radio Kreiz Breizh on radio, and Brezhoweb, France 3 Breizh, France 3 Iroise, TV Breizh and TV Rennes on television. The national anthem, *Bro Gozh ma Zadoù*, is based on the Welsh *Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau*; the Dukes of Brittany's motto was *Kentoc'h mervel eget bezañ saotret* — "death before dishonour".

## Language & religion

Breton is an Insular Celtic language of the Brittonic branch, closely related to Cornish and more distantly to Welsh, and more distantly still to extinct Continental Celtic languages such as Gaulish. It has four main dialects — *Gwenedeg* (Vannes), *Kerneveg* (Cornouaille), *Leoneg* (Léon) and *Tregerieg* (Trégor) — of varying mutual intelligibility; a standard orthography was devised in 1908 and extended to Gwenedeg in the reform of 1941. Breton is now spoken mainly in Lower Brittany, by around 206,000 people as of 2013; a 2024 study found 2.7% of those surveyed, about 107,000 people, spoke it very well or fairly well. Eastern Brittany speaks *Gallo*, a Romance langue d'oïl. Breton was banned from French schools from 1880 until the Deixonne Law of 1951. Bretons are predominantly Catholic, with minorities in the Reformed Church of France and non-religious people.

## Overview

The Bretons are a Celtic people who settled in Brittany from the 3rd to 9th centuries, originally from south-western Great Britain. Their traditional language is Brezhoneg, a Brittonic Celtic language related to Cornish and Welsh. Brittany has been counted as one of the six Celtic nations, and its festival, pilgrimage and music traditions remain among the most actively practised folk cultures in France. France does not collect statistics on ethnicity, so the exact number of Bretons cannot be established.

## Material culture

Breton material culture is documented mainly through 19th- and early-20th-century garments of wool decorated with thread, beads and metal.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Breton textiles are known from 19th-century wool garments worked with coloured thread, metal and glass beads.

- **Beaded and metal-thread woollens** — Jackets, vests, bodices and skirts of wool decorated with wool thread, metal thread and glass beads.
- **Silk-lined jackets and vests** — 19th-century jackets and vests pairing wool with silk, without beadwork.
- **Decorative ribbons** — Silk ribbons worked with metal spangles that trimmed garments.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress consists of matching ensembles of wool bodices, skirts and jackets with metal and beaded decoration, worn in ceremonial contexts.

- **Leather and brass belt** (*gouriz*) — A belt of leather and brass dated about 1834.

### Architecture

The main built features documented are the shrines and parish churches of the seven founder saints, which anchor the Tro Breizh pilgrimage.

- **Saint-Pol-de-Léon** (*Kastell-Paol*) — Shrine of one of the seven founder saints.
- **Tréguier** (*Landreger*) — Shrine of one of the seven founder saints.

The only documented metalwork object is the gouriz belt, though metal appears widely as costume decoration.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Breton body adornment is documented only through metal thread, paillettes and spangles applied to garments and ribbons.

## Music & performance

Breton music features a cappella choral singing and instrumental music with characteristic bagpipes and oboe-like instruments.

- **Choral singing tradition** (*kan ha diskan*) — A choral a cappella tradition that is a main type of Breton music.
- **Oboe-like instrument** (*bombard*) — A characteristic traditional instrument similar to an oboe.
- **Bagpipe** (*veuze*) — One of two kinds of traditional Breton bagpipe.
- **Small bagpipe** (*binioù kozh*) — A traditional Breton bagpipe displaced in many settings after the Second World War.
- **Large bagpipe** (*binioù bras*) — Became commonplace after the Second World War through Breton pipe bands.

## Dance & theatre

Breton dances are performed mainly in circles and chains at fest-noz festivals, with some reaching back to the Middle Ages.

- **Gavotte dances** (*gavottes*) — Among the best-known Breton dances.

The Breton festival year centres on pardons, the feast days of parish patron saints, and the major pilgrimage tour of Brittany.

Breton cooking draws from French tradition with distinctive local specialities of crêpes, pastries, puddings and regional drinks.

## Overview

The Aromanians (*Armãnji*, *Rrãmãnji*) are an ethnic group native to the southern Balkans who speak Aromanian, an Eastern Romance language descended from the Vulgar Latin of the Romanized Balkans. In Greece they live mainly in Epirus, Macedonia, Thessaly and Aetolia-Acarnania — in the Pindus Mountains, around Olympus and Vermion, and near the Prespa Lakes on the Albanian and North Macedonian border — in upland settlements such as Samarina (*Samarina*, *Xamarina* or *San Marina*), Perivoli (*Pirivoli*) and Smixi (*Zmixi*), and in towns including Metsovo (*Aminciu*), Ioannina (*Ianina*, *Enina*, *Enãna*), Veria (*Veryia*), Grevena (*Grebini*), Trikala (*Trikolj*), Katerini, Agrinio (*Vrachori*) and Thessaloniki (*Sãruna*). Estimates of their number in Greece range from 40,000 to 300,000; the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne put it at 150,000–200,000, while the 1940 and 1951 censuses recorded 26,750 and 22,736 Vlachs. Thede Kahl estimates fewer than 100,000 fluent speakers. They are widely known by the medieval exonym "Vlachs", and are recognised in Greece as a linguistic rather than an ethnic minority.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The objects in this atlas are a woman's festive costume and a few household weavings, and they define what the sources let us say about Aromanian pattern.

**Tapestry-woven aprons** — Aprons built from two equal loom-widths of wool joined along a selvedge to give a horizontal seam, woven tabby (weft-faced) and in tapestry technique. One is predominantly dark red, with isolated elongated diamonds in the centre field and a deep border of linked zigzags; another is dark blue with diamond and zigzag bands at the sides and lower half. Both carry blue, green, maroon and black woollen yarns worked together with gold- and silver-metal-wrapped thread, and all four sides are finished with applied commercial wool braiding and a braided tie.

**Plain-ground wool aprons** — A near-square apron of deep yellow hand-spun, hand-woven wool with a single band of white geometric ornament near the base, its edges bordered in white wool stitching, the hem carrying an added knotted cotton fringe and the ties plaited from yellow and white wool.

**Patterned knitted socks** — Knee-length women's socks knitted in the round in a slight variant of western stocking stitch, in bands of white, red, blue and black wool with gold-coloured metal-wrapped thread, the top third left in natural cream and closed with three rows of garter stitch and plied yarn ties. A second, plainer pair is hand-knitted from hand-spun black and blue wool, each blue band framed by a darned line of gold-coloured metal-wrapped thread that stops short of the sole.

**Panelled fulled-wool outer garments** — Sleeveless coats and waistcoats cut from heavily fulled twill wool and assembled from very large numbers of separate panels — fourteen at the back of one black coat, twenty-two in a dark red waistcoat falling just below the knee — to produce a flared, heavy skirt. The square or deep U-shaped necklines carry dense couched wool braiding, predominantly maroon or black with blue, green and orange wool and yellow and green silk highlights; braiding is repeated at armholes, hem and pocket openings, and one waistcoat has an inscription above the pleated skirt.

**Beaded bib (plastron)** — A rectangle of natural cream twill cloth gathered onto a blue cotton velvet neckband, decorated in a V-shape at the centre top with small transparent, blue, green and red glass beads, gold and black faceted beads, a line of silver-coloured metal sequins, blue and black rickrack and polychrome tubular glass beads.

**Striped hand-spun household weaving** — Utility cloth in undyed and dyed sheep's wool: a narrow bag with red and black stripes, recycled from a larger shepherd's bag and fitted with a plaited wool carrying string, and a tabby-woven napkin of natural undyed wool with narrow stripes of supplementary weft in red and dark blue, edged all round in red wool blanket chain stitch and tied with a twisted red-and-white cord.

**Motif vocabulary.** Isolated elongated diamonds (apron centre fields), linked zigzags (deep apron borders), diamond-and-zigzag bands (apron sides), vertical lines with dashes (apron side borders), a band of white geometric ornament (yellow apron), narrow supplementary-weft stripes (napkin, bag), and the V-shaped beaded panel of the plastron.

### Clothing & dress

In Aromanian rural areas clothing differed from city dress, and the shape and colour of a garment, the volume of the headgear and the shape of a jewel could indicate both cultural affiliation and the specific village a wearer came from. Women's festive attire, as represented here, is layered: a calf-length long-sleeved chemise of beige tabby cotton muslin with natural cream seersucker stripes, cut from four full 36.5 cm weaving widths for a straight line, opening vertically at the centre front to below the bust and trimmed with cream, black and dark blue crocheted silk; over it the beaded plastron at the throat, a pleated tapestry-woven apron, patterned knee-length socks, and a panelled sleeveless coat or waistcoat of fulled wool. Summer footwear is *opanci* — shoes of sewn and plaited dark brown, tan and red-brown leather, a one-piece sole-and-toe sewn up the centre of the toe, black straps across the front and a deep red strap threaded through a suede heel rim and fastened with a metal buckle. For men, the sources record the *fustanella*, whose use among Aromanians can be traced to at least the 15th century — notably on the Aromanian *stećak* of the Radimlja necropolis — and which Aromanians claim as their ethnic costume.

### Architecture

The sources used here say nothing about Aromanian house form, building materials or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources document no Aromanian ceramic or metalworking tradition; the everyday objects they record are textile. Hand-spun, hand-woven wool serves both carriage and table: a long narrow striped container cut down from a full-sized shepherd's bag, with a small plaited wool carrying string at one side, and a single-loom-width napkin of undyed sheep's wool hemmed top and bottom and finished with blanket chain stitching and a twisted cord. Metal enters the costume rather than the household — gold- and silver-metal-wrapped thread woven into aprons and darned onto socks, silver-coloured sequins on the plastron, and a buckle on the *opanci*.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources note only that the shape of a jewel, like the cut of a garment or the bulk of a headdress, could mark cultural affiliation and village origin; they name no jewelry types, materials or ritual functions, and record no tattooing, henna or hair practices. The nearest documented adornment is sewn rather than worn: the glass, faceted and tubular beads, sequins and rickrack massed in a V on the festive plastron and repeated along its velvet neckband.

## Music & performance

Polyphonic music is common among the Aromanians and follows a common set of rules. The sources name no instruments, song genres or performance occasions, and note that the Aromanian language is almost totally absent from television and that there are no exclusively Aromanian newspapers; the largest Aromanian cultural gatherings in the world are the festivals held at Metsovo, which regularly draw over 40,000 participants.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Aromanian dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The Aromanians are predominantly Orthodox Christians and follow the Eastern Orthodox liturgical calendar; the sources describe no life-cycle rites, though the museum records repeatedly distinguish "festive attire" and "festive costume" from everyday dress, implying a calendar of occasions at which the beaded plastron, metal-threaded aprons and heavy panelled coats were worn. The one dated observance is national rather than agrarian. The Ottoman Empire recognised the Aromanians as a distinct millet, the Ullah millet, on 22 May 1905, with freedoms of worship and education in their own language; the date of the announcement of the irade, 23 May 1905, has in recent times been adopted as **Aromanian National Day** (*Dzua Natsionalã a Armãnjilor*) by Aromanians in Albania, Australia, Bulgaria and North Macedonia — but notably not in Greece or among Aromanians in the Greek diaspora. In Romania the same event is marked on 10 May as Balkan Romanianness Day, an observance extended to the Megleno-Romanians and Istro-Romanians as well. Greek Aromanians took part instead in the Greek Struggle for Independence and are commemorated through that national history; the Metsovo festivals are the principal recurring Aromanian cultural event the sources record.

## Foodways

Aromanian cuisine is strongly influenced by Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisine. The sources used name no staple grains, dishes, ceremonial foods or drink traditions.

## Oral tradition & literature

A literature in the Aromanian language exists, and its written tradition is bound up with the Aromanians' position inside the Greek-dominated Rum millet: the first book written in Aromanian used the Greek alphabet and was aimed at spreading Greek among Aromanian-speakers. The Latin-derived character of the language began to be studied in grammars and language booklets in the early 19th century; the work many scholars have called the most valuable for translating the ethnic name is the grammar printed in Vienna in 1813 by Mihail G. Boiagi, titled *Γραμματική Ρωμαϊκή ήτοι Μακεδονοβλαχική / Romanische oder Macedonowlachische Sprachlehre* ("Romance or Macedono-Vlach Grammar"). The term "Aromanian" itself was coined by Gustav Weigand in *Die Aromunen* (1894). Preservation work in Greece is recent and contested: since 1994 the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki has offered beginner and advanced courses in "Koutsovlach"; in 1997 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe passed Recommendation 1333 urging Balkan states to address the "critical situation" of Aromanian culture and language, after which President Konstantinos Stefanopoulos publicly urged Greek Aromanians to teach the language to their children. Of more than 200 Vlach cultural associations active in Greece as of 2002, many do not even carry the term "Vlach" in their titles and only a few work on the language.

## Language & religion

Aromanian is an Eastern Romance language, very similar to Romanian, with many slightly varying dialects; it developed from Common Romanian, the shared stage of the Eastern Romance varieties that evolved out of the Vulgar Latin spoken by Paleo-Balkan peoples. It shares features with Albanian, Bulgarian and Greek and has many Greek, Slavic and Turkish loanwords, but its lexicon remains majority Romance. Thede Kahl divides speakers into two main groups with sub-groups: the **Rrãmãnji** (Muzãchiars, Fãrshãrots, Moscopolitans) and the **Armãnji** (Pindeans of the Pindus, Gramustians of the Gramos mountains). Greek Aromanians, nicknamed *Koutsovlachs*, are predominantly Orthodox Christians following the Eastern Orthodox calendar; before the 19th century they were subsumed, as Orthodox Christians, into the Rum millet under the Patriarchate of Constantinople, and most still consider themselves part of the broader Greek nation (*Elini*).

## Sources & further reading

- Gustav Weigand, *Die Aromunen* (1894) — the work in which the term "Aromanian" was coined.
- Mihail G. Boiagi, *Romanische oder Macedonowlachische Sprachlehre* (Vienna, 1813) — the early grammar of the language.
- Thede Kahl — German scholar of Aromanian studies, source of the Rrãmãnji/Armãnji classification and of the current speaker estimates.
- Tom Winnifrith — on Vlach origins, population figures and Aromanian-language schooling in Albania.
- Bosch et al. (2006) — genetic study concluding the Aromanians are genetically indistinguishable from other Balkan populations.
- Wikipedia, "Aromanians": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aromanians
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: no inscription for this group was among the sources used.
- Smithsonian Folkways search: https://folkways.si.edu/search?query=Aromanian
- British Museum online collection (holder of the costume and household weavings shown here): https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection

Aromanian cuisine is strongly influenced by Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisine, though specific staples and dishes are not documented.

## Oral tradition & literature

An Aromanian literary tradition exists from the 19th century, beginning with works using the Greek alphabet and developing through linguistic and educational texts.

- **Romanische oder Macedonowlachische Sprachlehre** (*grammar*) — A grammar printed in Vienna in 1813 by Mihail G. Boiagi, called by many scholars the most valuable for translating the ethnic name.
- **Die Aromunen** (*work*) — Published in 1894 by Gustav Weigand, the work in which the term Aromanian was coined.

## Language & religion

Aromanian is an Eastern Romance language with many Greek, Slavic and Turkish loanwords, divided into the Rrãmãnji and Armãnji groups, and speakers are predominantly Orthodox Christians.

- **Eastern Romance language** (*Aromanian*) — Very similar to Romanian, it developed from Common Romanian and the Vulgar Latin spoken by Paleo-Balkan peoples.
- **Rrãmãnji speakers** (*Rrãmãnji*) — One main group of Aromanian speakers, divided into Muzãchiars, Fãrshãrots, and Moscopolitans.
- **Armãnji speakers** (*Armãnji*) — One main group of Aromanian speakers, divided into Pindeans of the Pindus and Gramustians of the Gramos mountains.

## Glossary

- *Armãnji* — One main group of Aromanian speakers, including Pindeans and Gramustians
- *Rrãmãnji* — One main group of Aromanian speakers, including Muzãchiars, Fãrshãrots, and Moscopolitans
- *Vlachs* — Medieval exonym for Aromanians, still used widely
- *opanci* — Sewn leather shoes with a one-piece sole-and-toe and metal buckle
- *fustanella* — Traditional male ethnic costume, traceable to at least the 15th century
- *plastron* — Beaded bib worn at the throat with beads, sequins and rickrack decoration
- *stećak* — Medieval tombstone, as seen at Radimlja necropolis
- *tapestry technique* — Weaving method using weft-faced wool to create patterns
- *tabby* — Plain weave textile structure
- *Dzua Natsionalã a Armãnjilor* — Aromanian National Day, celebrated on 23 May
- *Ullah millet* — Ottoman administrative designation for Aromanians recognized in 1905
- *Common Romanian* — Shared stage of Eastern Romance varieties that evolved from Vulgar Latin
- *Eastern Romance* — Language family including Aromanian, Romanian, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian
- *Vulgar Latin* — Common Latin spoken by ordinary people in the Romanized Balkans

## Sources & further reading

- Gustav Weigand, Die Aromunen (1894) — the work in which the term "Aromanian" was coined.

title: "Tehuelche"
subtitle: "Argentina"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Tehuelche, who call themselves *Aónikenk*, are an Indigenous people of eastern Patagonia in South America, historically ranging across the plateaus and river valleys between the Strait of Magellan and the Colorado and Río Negro rivers, with the Chubut River dividing the two largest subdivisions recognised by most specialists — "Southern" and "Northern" Tehuelche. Their language belongs to the Chonan family, alongside Teushen, Selkʼnam and Haush. Once nomadic hunters who followed guanaco herds between winter lowlands and the summer plateaus and Andean ranges, they were dispossessed in the nineteenth century by Argentine and Chilean colonisation, by the sheep estates established across Patagonia, and by introduced epidemic disease; most now live in the cities and towns of Argentine Patagonia. Argentina's 2010 census recorded 27,813 people identifying as Tehuelche. In folk-culture terms they matter as the makers of the painted guanaco-skin cloak and of the stone-and-cord hunting weapon that the earliest photographs of Patagonia show in use.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Quillango** — the painted cloak of sewn guanaco skins, named in the catalogue record of a nineteenth-century photograph of a Tehuelche chief who wears it wrapped about the body with a knife tucked into the waist. Museum photographs show the same skin cloak worn by men, by young men in studio portraits, and by women, who carried an infant in the back of it; it is the garment by which Tehuelche sitters are identified in the Patagonian photographic record.

**Ponchos of the trade fairs** — woven garments were among the goods exchanged at two important eighteenth-century fairs, at Cayrú in the western Tandilia system and at Chapaleofú, which the Jesuits of the period, Thomas Falkner among them, called "poncho fairs". Livestock, agricultural produce and garments moved there between the peoples of the humid Pampas, northern Patagonia and both flanks of the Andes, and the fairs were one engine of the cultural exchange between Tehuelche, Ranquel and Mapuche.

**Woven blankets** — photographic records describe Tehuelche women wrapped in a blanket or in a woven blanket rather than in skin, sometimes with a headband, in one case while riding a horse heavily loaded with goods.

The sources used name no motifs or pattern names for these textiles, so no motif vocabulary is given here.

### Clothing & dress

The documented dress is built around the guanaco-skin cloak. Men in the photographs wear a headband and the skin cloak, in one instance with ankle bands, and carry the stone-and-cord weapon in the hand with a knife at the waist of the cloak; another man appears with a headband, earrings and a guanaco cloak. Two figures leaning on a boat wear skin cloaks together with leggings, while four men in the distance behind them wear European clothing — a direct record of the period when the two wardrobes stood side by side. Women wear either a skin cloak or a woven blanket, with a headband, and necklaces appear in a portrait of a woman photographed alongside a Tehuelche boy. A boy is shown with a headband, a necklace and a wrap around the waist. Footwear is attested only indirectly and from the Spanish side: the explorers of 1520 were struck by footprints enlarged by the animal furs used as foot coverings, which is one account given for the name *Patagones*, "the big-footed", used by the Spaniards from Oviedo onward. The sources used do not distinguish a separate ceremonial costume.

### Architecture

Tehuelche groups were mobile but moved in defined circuits, predominantly west to east and back, and each season had its own camping places. The camps were called *aik* or *aiken* among the Tehuelche themselves and *tolderías* by the Spaniards and Creoles — a term and a way of living that the Mapuche subsequently adopted from them, one of the clearest cases of borrowing running from Tehuelche to Mapuche rather than the other way. Each group held specific hunting and gathering territories whose boundaries were fixed by inherited markers in the landscape — a hill, a trough, a hollow, an important tree — whose significance is not recorded; a group unable to meet its needs at home had to ask permission of neighbours of the same ethnic group to use their resources, and taking them without it meant war. Groups numbered between fifty and a hundred people. The sources used describe no house form, roof type or architectural ornament beyond the name of the camp itself.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Two object classes dominate the catalogued material. The hunting weapon of stone and cord — the *bolas* of the photographs, catalogued in Swedish as a *boleador* "for ostrich hunting" — is held in the hand of a chief and of a young man in studio portraits and survives as a collected specimen. The second is the stone knife: an old blade from Santa Cruz, worked from a flint-like stone into an elongated, rounded-triangular form, with fine edge retouch on one face only. Both belong to a much older lithic sequence in the region: the **Toldense industry** of some six thousand years ago, with two-sided sub-triangular projectile points, lateral and terminal scrapers, bifacial knives and bone tools, and the later **Casapedrense industry** of roughly 7000–4000 BC, with a higher proportion of blade tools, read as a specialisation in guanaco hunting that continues into later Tehuelche life. A boy photographed in shrubbery holds a bow and arrows with a pot or basket at his feet. The sources used record no ceramics or metalwork.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment is documented only through the photographs: headbands worn by men, women, a young man and a boy; earrings on a young man in a guanaco cloak; ankle bands, uncertainly identified, on a chief; and necklaces — two of them worn at once by a woman in a head-and-shoulders portrait, one by a boy. The sources used name no jewellery types, materials or ritual functions, and record no tattooing, body painting or hair practice.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Tehuelche instruments, song genres or musical performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Tehuelche dance or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

No annual festival calendar appears in the sources used. What they document is ritual life without an institutional frame: like other peoples without a state structure, the Tehuelche had no organised religious system with a liturgy and a vertical hierarchy, but held a body of belief in their own myths and rites, narrated and renewed by shamans who also practised medicine with the help of spirits invoked within themselves. Earth spirits were many, and above them stood a supreme being who made the world and does not intervene in it. Evil spirits called *guarichos* were part of the same world, and *Gualichu* is named as an evil spirit of the mythology. The one life-cycle rite the sources describe is marriage, and they describe it as a transaction within a strongly ordered family unit in which men held authority and women were subordinate: a father would offer his daughter in marriage in exchange for goods, and a man could have two or three wives according to his standing. The sources used do not cover birth, coming-of-age or funerary rites. Among sacred places, Mount Fitz Roy is named as one of the sites held sacred by groups who moved up to the central Patagonian plateaus or into the Andes in summer.

## Foodways

Tehuelche subsistence was hunting and gathering across the thicket steppes of Patagonia, with seasonal movement toward the guanaco herds: winters in the low ground — meadows, wetlands, shores and lake margins — and summers on the central plateaus or in the Andes. Guanaco and rhea meat, the rhea known as *ñandú* or *choique*, were the mainstays, followed by South Andean deer, deer, Patagonian mara, and even puma and jaguar, together with certain plants; cultivation was learned only late. Fish and shellfish were subject to rules rather than appetite — some groups prohibited eating fish outright. The adoption of the horse, known to them from about 1570 and in domestic use widely by the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries under Mapuche influence, remade this economy by remaking mobility: ancestral territories and movement patterns were both altered by it. The sources used name no prepared dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods or drink traditions.

## Oral tradition & literature

The narrative tradition recorded in the sources is cosmological. In one version of the creation myth the deity *Kóoch* brings order out of the world's chaos and creates its distinct elements; the Selkʼnam of Tierra del Fuego tell a parallel story of a world-maker named *Kénos'*, a variant of Kóoch through a common root, and in it a certain *El Lal* is sent. Within Tehuelche myth, through the god *Temauckel*, *Erral* created human beings and taught them the use of the bow and arrow. These narratives were carried and updated by shamans. Documentation and revival rest heavily on the last fluent speaker, Dora Manchado, who died in 2019; the language was recorded from her and has since been recuperated and revitalised by groups of Aonekkenk working with linguists and anthropologists. A revival programme named *Kkomshkn e wine awkkoi ʼaʼien* — "I am not ashamed of speaking Tehuelche" — works on spreading both language and culture. The sources used name no epic cycle, proverb collection or riddle tradition.

## Language & religion

Tehuelche — also *Aonekkenk* or *Aonekko ʼaʼien* — is a Chonan language, grouped with Teushen, Selkʼnam and Haush; it is nominative–accusative and marks the nominative but not the accusative, a pattern reported from only six languages worldwide. Within the wider "Tehuelche complex" the available evidence distinguishes six languages: the Chon group, the language of the Gününa küne (Puelche, also *Gününa yajüch*, often treated as an isolate), and Querandí; a transitional central Patagonian language, *Tehuesh* or *Téushenkenk*, was gradually displaced by Aonekkenk but survives in plateau place names, the province name Chubut deriving from *chupat*. Decline began with Mapuche expansion from the north, continued under Argentine and Chilean occupation of Patagonia and state-facilitated genocide, and accelerated as Spanish became dominant: from some 5,000 speakers around 1900 to 29 in 1983/84, four by 2000, two by 2012, and none after 2019. Religion remains as described above — Earth spirits, a non-intervening creator, and shamanic practice — with no organised structure.

## Sources & further reading

- Thomas Falkner, *A Description of Patagonia and the Adjoining Parts of South America* (1774) — the earliest systematic classification, introducing "Tehuelhets" and the Het peoples.
- George Chaworth Musters, *At Home with the Patagonians*, 2nd edition, London, 1873 — the source of the drawing of Tehuelche crossing the Río Limay held by the Museum of World Culture.
- Milcíades Vignati, *Las culturas indígenas de la Pampa* and *Las culturas indígenas de la Patagonia* (1936).
- Federico A. Escalada, *El complejo tehuelche. Estudio de etnografía patagónica* (1949) — the five-part classification, with names collected from Mapuche-speaking informants including Chief Ciriaco Chaquilla and Agustina Quilchaman de Manquel.
- Rodolfo Casamiquela, *Rectificaciones y ratificaciones hacia una interpretación definitiva del panorama etnológico de la Patagonia y área septentrional adyacente* (1965), *Un nuevo panorama etnológico del área pan-pampeana y patagónica adyacente* (1969), and *Bosquejo de una etnología de la provincia de Río Negro* (1985).
- Alcide d'Orbigny, *Voyage dans l'Amérique méridionale* (1826–1833); Tomás Harrington's Gününa küne vocabulary, published 1946.
- Language documentation and revival: the Tehuelche community site *kketo sh m ʼekot – lengua tehuelche*; *Qadeshiakk*, materials about the language; the Tehuelche entry in the Intercontinental Dictionary Series.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehuelche_people
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehuelche_language
- British Museum online collection (Patagonian photographic prints): https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection
