title: "Zapotec"
subtitle: "Mexico"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Zapotec — *Bën za* in Valley Zapotec, "People of the clouds" — are an Indigenous people of Mexico concentrated in the southern state of Oaxaca, with communities in neighbouring Puebla, Veracruz and Guerrero and, after decades of labour migration, in Mexico City, Los Angeles, California's Central Valley and New Jersey. Estimates put the present population at 400,000 to 650,000; the 2020 census counted about 500,000 speakers of a Zapotec language, 5.7% of them monolingual. The languages form a main branch of the Oto-Manguean family, grouped with Chatino as Zapotecan. Four regional divisions are recognised: the *istmeños* of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, the *serranos* of the Sierra Madre de Oaxaca, the southern Zapotec of the Sierra Sur, and the Central Valley Zapotec of the Y-shaped valleys of Etla, Ocotlán and Mitla around the Atoyac River. Their pre-Columbian civilisation, centred on Monte Albán, produced one of Mesoamerica's first writing systems.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Huipil** — The women's upper garment, in the two collected examples built from a rectangle with a cut neck opening. One is blue cotton printed with white flowers (catalogued as possibly Manchester cotton), lined with red cotton printed with white polka dots, the round neck bordered with machine-stitched red and yellow stripes and the edge carrying a band of red and yellow floral embroidery. A festive variant is made of organza with green brocade, with a lace collar, lace sleeves and lace hem all trimmed with red ribbon — imported industrial cloth and trim absorbed into an Indigenous cut.

**Blusa** — A white plain-weave blouse with short gathered sleeves from Oaxaca, satin-stitch embroidered in red, yellow, blue and green with flower motifs around the neckline front and back and on two patch pockets at the lower front, finished with a red yarn tassel below the neck opening.

**Falda** — A wrap skirt of two flared panels with ties, woven of red cotton with weft-stripe patterning in black, white, yellow and green. Two diagonal V-shaped fields and a rectangle along the lower edge are embroidered in satin stitch with geometric motifs in blue, orange, purple, yellow, green and white.

**Sashes and girdles** — Narrow bands woven on the backstrap loom with warp-patterned cotton: a white sash with brown and black edge stripes and a central geometric field read by the cataloguer as scorpions; another with a brown and black human dancer from the *Danza de la Pluma* on a yellow ground. Women's girdles use a red wool floating-warp geometric pattern down a white centre, or are woven of silk with stiffening strips carried in the weft for strength and a braided fringe.

**Rebozo** — A wool shawl woven on the backstrap loom, white-grounded with warp-patterned multicoloured stripes and warp fringe finger-knotted at each end.

**Morral** — A knitted wool shoulder bag in dark brown, worked with two mirror-image bird-like figures in white perched on a "T", with rows of letters — several reversed — running along the upper and lower edges.

**Chichicaxtle fibre** — A 1940s ethnographic photograph from the district of San Carlos Yautepec records the spinning of bark fibre of chichicaxtle, a thread source distinct from the cotton and wool of the loom traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** Floral sprays in satin stitch (blouse necklines, huipil borders); cut-out flowers and leaves on pottery walls; warp-patterned geometric fields including forms identified as scorpions; a single plumed dancer from the Danza de la Pluma; mirrored birds flanking a "T"; fish, scratched into gourd and modelled in clay; diagonal black bands on plaited palm baskets; edge stripes in brown, black, yellow and burgundy.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress in the collections combines the huipil or embroidered blusa with a wrapped falda, bound at the waist by a woven *girdle* or sash. The head is dressed with a *rodete*, a turban of black wool hair cords — two cord cables joined at one end and left as a long fringe at the other — and hair is also bound with ornaments of braided green wool wrapped in violet and orange silk, branching into multiple tassels. On the Isthmus the Juchiteca skirt and huipil constitute the recognised "native outfit", worn by women and by *muxes*, the third-gender members of Isthmus Zapotec communities. Men's festival dress appears in photographs of Oaxacan musicians, who perform in white clothing and sombreros. Clothing manufacture is itself a Zapotec trade: treadle sewing machines arrived around 1940 and from about 1960 women who had woven since pre-Columbian times began making and designing men's ready-made shirts and trousers for local and export markets. In the sixteenth century, Zapotec warfare used armour of cotton.

### Architecture

The Zapotecs were a sedentary people living in villages and towns, in houses built of stone and mortar. The monumental tradition is best documented at Monte Albán, founded on a mountain in the no-man's-land overlooking the three Central Valleys and the largest city in the southern Mexican highlands until about AD 700: its main plaza carries monumental buildings, ball courts and tombs, and the arrowhead-shaped Building J, the "Conquest Slab", is faced with more than forty carved stones bearing hieroglyphic place-glyphs and ruler heads. Religious building centred on the *yo hopèe*, "house of the vital force", where priests performed rites. Mitla, seat of the paramount priest, is known for its ruins, and other centres include Lambityeco, Dainzú, Yagul, San José Mogote, El Palmillo and Zaachila. Water engineering was part of the built landscape: canal irrigation drew on small streams, and a dam and canal on the south-eastern flank of the mountain carried water to Monte Albán, 400 metres above the valley floor. A tomb excavated in Oaxaca in January 2026 has a frieze of an owl's head over the burial-chamber entrance, polychrome murals of figures carrying bags of copal, and stone-carved guardians at the threshold. The sources do not describe present-day Zapotec house form.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The signature ware in the collections is burnished black pottery, one piece inscribed on the base "Dona Rosa SB coyotepec Oaxaca Mexico". Vessel forms include a round pot with three prongs on the base, a tapering neck and a flaring horizontal lip, its wall pierced with cut-out flowers and leaves; a second pot with flowers etched into the side; and an *olla* with orange slip, black firing marks across the lower half and a burnished sheen. Small modelled work is abundant: figurines and toys in the form of parrot, bird, lizard, lion, fish and turtle, with wings and eyes incised and vent holes pierced; whistles shaped as peacock, rooster and duck with the mouthpiece in the tail; and a toy flute of burnished black clay with four finger holes and a snake carved between them. Household equipment includes a gourd strainer, hollowed and pierced with small holes, its stained upper half scratched with fish; and palm baskets (*cesto de palma*) plaited in two-over-two twill over a square foundation with a round bottom and a rolled rim. Carved and painted wooden figures were made for sale at the Day of the Dead festival: a bullfighting group with a male spectator and a bull fitted with cane pieces to hold fireworks, a twisted-bodied horse and rider, and a female figure with a skull head whose spinal column shows between shirt and skirt. Hunting equipment survives in a 1948 photograph of Luis Sanchez, described as the last blowgun maker of Oaxaca de Juárez, demonstrating his *cerbatana*.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Monte Albán's tombs and grave goods included finely worked gold jewelry, and Zapotec and Mixtec artisans resident in the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan fashioned jewelry for the *tlatoanis*, Moctezuma II among them. A dedication cache in Mound III at the Cuilapan Temple Pyramid, dated to AD 700, held many jade beads, two jade earspools, three obsidian blades, shells, stones, a pearl and small bird bones; jade was valued for its scarcity and worked by elite artists, obsidian blades belonged to bloodletting, and shell and pearl stood for the underworld. Present-day adornment in the collections is ceramic and fibre rather than metal: a necklace strung from seven burnished black pottery birds alternating with black pottery fish, the wool and silk hair tassels, and the *rodete* hair cords.

## Music & performance

Zapotec music appears in the sources chiefly through performance context rather than organology. A set of black-and-white photographs from Oaxaca shows a line of musicians in white clothing and sombreros playing their instruments in an open space outside a large building, accompanying dancers in elaborate painted-feather headdresses, with crowds of spectators and, at one edge, a seated official in uniform with a sabre. The sources do not name the instruments played. Pottery whistles and a toy flute with four finger holes, both in burnished black ware, document sound-making objects of the household. One distinct vocal-adjacent practice is recorded: whistling, used by Zapotec people to communicate in a way their colonizers would not detect — a practice that sits alongside the tonal structure of the languages themselves, where up to four tonemes distinguish meaning and tones are used for word play. Zapotec-language broadcasting is extensive: the CDI stations XEGLO at Guelatao de Juárez and XEQIN-AM at San Quintín in Baja California carry Zapotec programming, and on the Isthmus the commercial Radio TEKA (1030 AM) is joined by community stations, most notably Radio Totopo (102.5 FM) in Juchitán and Radio Atempa in San Blas Atempa.

## Dance & theatre

The one named dance in the sources is the **Danza de la Pluma**, whose plumed dancer is woven as a figure into the central band of a backstrap-loom sash — a dance important enough to become a textile motif. The Oaxaca photographs show its performance setting: dancers in elaborate headdresses of painted feathers, at times turned to face one another, at times facing the musicians, in the open space before a large building and ringed by spectators. Dance has a specific social function in the segregation of the sexes that structures much Zapotec social life: men and women work separately and remain apart during ritual occasions except when dancing. The *velas* of the Isthmus are the reference point for public assembly — political demonstrations organised by the Coalición Obrera Campesina Estudiantil del Istmo are described as resembling them. The sources used do not describe a Zapotec theatre or puppet tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The major pilgrimage named in the sources is to the *Virgen de Juquila*, a Marian devotion founded at Santa Catarina Juquila in Oaxaca; many Zapotec Catholics travel annually to visit the statue during festivities running from 7 to 9 December. The Day of the Dead festival is attested materially rather than descriptively: carved wooden horses and riders were made for sale at it, and a skull-headed female figurine was carved under its inspiration. Pre-Hispanic ritual included dedication of buildings by cache — the Cuilapan Temple Pyramid cache of jade, obsidian, shell, pearl and bird bone, dedicating the structure to power, sacrifice and the link between underworld and cosmos — and there is evidence for human sacrifice in some rites. Church and state were not separate at the conquest: a Zapotec lord was required to be trained in religious practice before taking power, and the priests, *Copa pitào*, were drawn mostly from the nobility, with commoners admitted only to the lower ranks. Life-cycle practice is documented at both ends. Burial of the dead with valuables survives from ancient usage. Marriage is monogamous in value, women are generally free to choose partners, and in some communities the bloody sheet from the wedding night is publicly displayed — a Mediterranean custom brought by the Spaniards. Muxes commonly take on caregiving in the household, including remaining at home to care for elderly parents, and one account describes a young *mayordomo* treated with complete deference.

## Foodways

The Central Valleys are considered one of the cradles of maize, and maize is correspondingly central to Zapotec religion: the primary god of the Valley Zapotecs, *Pitao Cozobi*, was the god of maize and agriculture, and *Coqui Lao* was god of turkey hens. The agricultural year runs against a dry season from November to May; along the rivers it is possible to plant and harvest twice, and canal irrigation extended cultivation to fields away from the Atoyac, with crops also grown on less fertile foothill soils as Monte Albán's population grew. Farming innovation produced enough surplus to pay tribute to the Spanish conquerors and still feed the population through natural disaster and epidemic. Spanish settlers introduced animals unknown in Oaxaca before — horses, cows, goats, sheep, chickens, mules and oxen. Wild game was taken with the blowgun, still made in Oaxaca de Juárez in the 1940s. Labour around food was sharply gendered: men carried out planting and plowing, women weeded and harvested and, above all, supplied male workers with food during agricultural work, alongside the household duties of cooking and child care. The exonym *Zapotec* itself derives, on the long-standing reading, from Nahuatl *tzapotēcah*, "inhabitants of the place of sapote", though recent UNAM work argues for a hybrid form from *za* (cloud) and *pochteca* (merchant). The sources used do not name specific Zapotec dishes or beverages.

## Oral tradition & literature

Several origin legends are recorded, none transcribed before the Spanish conquest. In one, the Zapotec are the original people of the valley of Oaxaca, born from rocks or descended from big cats — pumas, jaguars and ocelots. In another they settled the Oaxaca valley after founding the Toltec empire and descend from the people of Chicomoztoc. Contemporary and historical Zapotec accounts have ancestors emerging from the earth or from caves, or turning into people from trees or jaguars, while the governing elite held that they descended from supernatural beings living among the clouds and would return to the clouds at death — the belief behind the self-designation *Be'ena' Za'a*, the Cloud People. Written tradition is old and interrupted: a logosyllabic script, one of Mesoamerica's first, with a glyph per syllable, is attested from about 500 BC on the Danzante stone (Monument 3) from San José Mogote and went out of use in the late Classic period; it remains undeciphered apart from calendar signs. Franciscan or Dominican friars published a vocabulary and grammar of Antequera Zapotec in the sixteenth century, the Isthmus Zapotec alphabet in use today was founded in the 1950s from work reaching back to the 1920s, and contemporary literature in Zapotec has been written by Irma Pineda, Natalia Toledo and Felipe Lopez. Andrés Henestrosa was a Zapotec scholar of the language and culture.

## Language & religion

Zapotec is a close-knit family of around fifty to sixty varieties in the Oto-Manguean stock, with a time depth comparable to the Romance languages; many varieties are mutually unintelligible and the Mexican government officially recognises sixty. Names for the language vary locally — *Diidxazá* in Juchitán, *Didxsaj* in Mitla, *Diža'xon* in Zoogocho, *Di'zhke'* in Coatec, *Dí'zdéh* in Miahuatec, *Tiits Së* in Santa Catarina Quioquitani — the first element meaning 'word'. All varieties are tonal and all contrast phonation types in vowels. Viability varies sharply: Loxicha Zapotec has over 70,000 speakers while San Agustín Mixtepec Zapotec reportedly has one. The Zapotec are now largely Catholic, with older practice visible inside it: San Pedro resembles the rain god *Cocijo*, and the dead are still buried with valuables. The pre-conquest religion was polytheistic, built around *pè*, the life force residing in wind and breath, with deities including Cocijo, *Pitao Cozaana*, *Pitao Hichaana*, *Pitao Pezelao*, *Copijcha*, *Coquihani* and *Pitao Xicala*, and a hierarchy topped by the *ouija-tào*, the great seer, who resided at Mitla.

## Overview

The Zapotec are an Indigenous people concentrated in Oaxaca, Mexico, with a population of 400,000 to 650,000 speakers across multiple regional varieties. Their pre-Columbian civilization centred on Monte Albán produced one of Mesoamerica's first writing systems. The Zapotec languages form a main branch of the Oto-Manguean family, with regional divisions including the istmeños, serranos, southern Zapotec, and Central Valley Zapotec. Today they are largely Catholic, though older religious practices remain visible.

## Material culture

Zapotec material culture centres on textiles made on the backstrap loom, burnished black pottery, and carved wooden objects, with Spanish colonial influences absorbed into Indigenous forms.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Backstrap-loom weaving produces patterned cotton and wool textiles in distinctive geometric and figural motifs.

- **Huipil** — A women's upper garment built from a rectangle with a cut neck opening, made of blue cotton with white flowers or organza with green brocade and imported lace and ribbon.
- **Falda** — A wrap skirt of two flared panels woven of red cotton with weft-stripe patterning, embroidered with geometric motifs in multiple colours.
- **Rebozo** — A wool shawl woven on the backstrap loom with warp-patterned multicoloured stripes and finger-knotted warp fringe.
- **Morral** — A knitted wool shoulder bag in dark brown worked with mirror-image bird-like figures in white and rows of letters along the edges.
- **Sashes and girdles** — Narrow bands woven on the backstrap loom with warp-patterned cotton or silk, some carrying geometric motifs identified as scorpions or dancers from the Danza de la Pluma.

### Clothing & dress

Women combine the huipil or embroidered blusa with a wrapped falda, bound by a woven girdle or sash, and dress the head with a rodete and braided wool ornaments.

- **Rodete** — A turban of black wool hair cords joined at one end and left as a long fringe at the other.
- **Blusa** — A white plain-weave blouse with short gathered sleeves, satin-stitch embroidered in multiple colours with flower motifs and finished with a red yarn tassel.
- **Juchiteca skirt and huipil** (*Juchiteca*) — On the Isthmus, the recognised native outfit worn by women and by muxes, the third-gender members of Isthmus Zapotec communities.

- **Mitla** — Seat of the paramount priest, known for its ruins.

## Overview

The Rarámuri, called Tarahumara by the Spanish from the 1500s onward, are an Indigenous people of the state of Chihuahua in northern Mexico. Once spread across much of Chihuahua, they withdrew on the arrival of Spanish colonizers in the 16th century into the high sierras and canyons of the Sierra Madre Occidental — including the Copper Canyon — and the part of that range they now occupy is often called the Sierra Rarámuri. Estimates put their number in 2006 at between 50,000 and 70,000. Their language belongs to the Uto-Aztecan family and is the second most widely spoken member of it after Nahuatl. In folk-culture terms they are known above all for prayer and communication through long-distance running, for a religion that reworked Catholic figures into Indigenous ones with little outside supervision, and for the brewing and sharing of maize beer that organizes nearly every collective occasion.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

Rarámuri weaving in the collections shown here is overwhelmingly narrow-band work: sashes and belts whose patterning is carried entirely in the warp, so the design appears as lengthwise bands, lozenges and waves rather than as a woven-in picture.

**Natépare** — A broad woven wool sash. Documented examples set geometric figures, including zigzags, in dark brown or black against undyed white, and frame them with a border that runs the whole length of the band in red, black, orange and blue; both ends finish in a fringe of interlaced warp threads. The wool is handspun and the belts are long enough to wrap the body several times.

**Faja** — The wool belt type in its wider form, with parallel bands of brown, orange, blue, red, yellow or green flanking a central field in brown and white that carries an undulating wave pattern, sometimes alternating straight and wavy stripes toward the ends. Some examples combine undyed handspun wool warps with commercial synthetic plied yarns in blue, red, pink and green — a sign of how industrial thread entered an otherwise domestic technique.

**Ceñidor** — The narrow cotton band, woven in mercerized cotton rather than wool: a single coloured stripe on each side of a centre field of alternating transverse blocks (white and green, yellow and green, red and green, blue and orange). The warps at both ends are gathered into two plaited fringes that end in a tassel.

**Tira** — The museum term used for these woven bands as a class, recorded alongside *faja* and *ceñidor* for the same objects, indicating that one narrow-band technique served several belt widths and functions.

**Telar** — The band loom itself was collected as an object. A British Museum man's sash is described as ring-woven on a rigid horizontal loom with handspun wool, with the end of the weaving above the fringe reinforced by a line of twining.

**Motif vocabulary.** Warp-patterned diamond or lozenge in the centre field, usually brown and white; zigzag; a central wave or undulating line; alternating transverse blocks read as a checkerboard; parallel lengthwise stripes framing the centre field; a continuous border band running the full length; plaited or interlaced warp fringes finished with tassels.

### Clothing & dress

The dress represented in collections is built around the loose cotton blouse, *blusa*, made for men, women and children alike, and the woven belt. A man's blouse of red cotton printed with small yellow, blue and purple flowers has a round neck without a collar, a vertical band down the centre of the chest from neck to below the waist with the fabric turned reverse-side out, pleats on either side of that band, balloon sleeves, and white buttons at the neck opening and cuffs. Another is cut from unbleached sheeting with a shoulder yoke, cuffs and hem binding of the same red floral cotton, pleats below the yoke front and back, and a purple button moulded with a flower. Children's blouses follow the adult pattern in orange or pink cotton with contrasting yokes, cuffs, short standing collars and hem bindings, fastened with mismatched buttons and snaps. Over these go the *natépare* and *faja* sashes. Footwear is the *huarache*, the sandal worn for running, which scientific and journalistic writing on Rarámuri endurance has made a byword in minimalist-running circles. Ceremonial dress is distinct: *matachín* dancers appear lavishly dressed in colorful attire that observers have compared to North African garments.

### Architecture

The sources are thin on building form. Most Rarámuri still practice a traditional lifestyle that includes inhabiting natural shelters — caves and cliff overhangs — in the canyon country, and almost all households move from one place to another over the course of a year, many of them practising transhumance with cattle, sheep and goats. The structures the sources do name are built collectively: granaries, houses and corrals raised by neighbours working together, the work party itself being one of the occasions for which maize beer is brewed. The other built landscape in Rarámuri territory is the mission: Juan Fonte's San Pablo Balleza at the southern edge of the territory, later foundations at Las Bocas, Huejotitán, San Felipe and Satevó, the mission of San Francisco de Borja destroyed in the 1648 war, and the Spanish Villa de Aguilar planted in the heart of the upper country afterward. Nothing in the sources used describes roof types, wall construction or architectural ornament.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Rarámuri pottery is lightly fired and fire-stained earthenware. The recurring form is a round pot with a flat bottom tapering to a short vertical neck, sometimes with a looped handle on either side and a separate lid shaped like an onion, pierced through the top; decoration is painted directly on the body — white flowers around the neck and white dots on the lid, or orange flowers with an orange band and zigzag line at the rim — and one example has large incised lines across the base. Museum records keep the Spanish names for the vessel classes: *jarro* for the bellied jar, *vasija* for a clay vessel generally, and *jícara* for a wide fired-clay bowl with traces of red painted decoration, heavily sooted on the outside, which its collector reported was used for roasting maize. Basketry is equally characteristic: double-walled baskets plaited from pine needles with a square base flaring out to a rounded rim, double-walled basketry mugs with serrated lips and a looped handle, and a lidded double-walled basket plaited from yucca or sotol fibre.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment in these collections is glass-bead work, recorded under Spanish names. *Collar de chaquira* describes a bundle of eight bead necklaces, each in several colours, bound together with a brown-red cotton band. A single *collar* is strung as a long repeating sequence: a run of white beads, then five red and five blue, then white again. *Aretes de chaquira*, bead earrings, combine red, blue and white beads terminating in a larger angular white bead, hung from white-metal fittings. Beyond beadwork the sources mention metal only through an individual: Xemexe Tierrablanca is listed among notable Rarámuri as a silversmith, photographer and musician. The sources used say nothing about tattooing, body painting or hair practices.

## Music & performance

Music is not an occasional art among the Rarámuri but a frame for ordinary conduct; the classical pianist Romayne Wheeler, who has written about them, puts it as "Music sanctifies the moment in the life of all the Tarahumaras" and "All of our actions have musical meaning." The instrument at the centre of it is the violin, played through the end-of-year cycle and masterfully carved but left unvarnished. Collected examples are carved of wood with an hour-glass body, f-holes cut on either side of the strings, a bridge and two wire strings fastened to pegs at the head; the Metropolitan Museum records one under the Rarámuri name *raberi*, made of yellow pine with horsehair. The pieces played in this season are known as *matachín* tunes and accompany dancing, with rattles called *sáuraka*. During Lent the instruments change: three-holed flutes of river cane are played together with drums. Also collected are *matraca* rattles — a stick handle with a cog near the end and a perpendicular piece of wood whose flap rests on the cog, the wood decorated with burnt S-shapes or burnt circles around the edge — classed in the museum record as religious and ritual equipment. At the drinking gatherings described below, the music is fiddles, flutes, drums and guitars. Rarámuri-language radio is broadcast by station XETAR from Guachochi, Chihuahua.

## Dance & theatre

Music and dance are described as highly integrated into Rarámuri social life, and the named dance tradition is the ***matachín***: dancers in elaborate, brightly coloured costume moving to violin tunes during the end-of-year cycle, accompanied by *sáuraka* rattles. Dancing also belongs to the beer-centred gatherings, where it goes on alongside the fiddles, flutes, drums and guitars. The other patterned public performances are competitive rather than theatrical. In *rarajipari* — translated as 'foot throwing' — teams of men kick a wooden ball as they run, relaying it to the next runner while teammates move ahead to the following relay point; races run from a few hours to a couple of days without a break. Women's races use a stick and hoop. Collections hold the equipment: wooden balls carved for use in a throwing game, catalogued as game-balls and sporting equipment. Footraces appear in the sources under the names *rarajípare* and *ariwete*. The sources used do not describe a masked or puppet theatre.

## Festivals & rituals

The Rarámuri ceremonial year is organized around the fermented maize drink *batári* (Spanish *tesgüino*) and the gatherings called *tesgüinadas*. These include rain fiestas, harvest ceremonies, curing fiestas, the Guadalupe Fiesta, Holy Week, races and Sunday gatherings. Many fall in the winter post-harvest season, when sharing beer between neighbouring communities renews social ties; rain and harvest ceremonies fall within the farming months to secure the crop. Others arise directly out of collective labour — the work parties called *nateba*, when neighbours help one family with its fields or raise a granary, house or corral. Each event requires a shaman, a *curandero* or a chanter: the *curandero* diagnoses and heals the sick, while chanters lead the community in the chants and rhythms that carry the ceremony. The religious obligations around the drink are precise. An *olla* of *batári* must be dedicated to Onorúame before anyone drinks from it, and during a curing ceremony the *olla* rests in front of a cross until the rite ends; some rituals run as long as 48 hours. The one life-cycle rite the sources name is a coming-of-age: at fourteen a boy is allowed to drink *batári* for the first time, after a short sermon about his responsibilities as a man. The anthropologist John Kennedy called the whole institution the "tesgüino network" and reckoned that the average Tarahumara spends at least 100 days a year directly concerned with the drink or under its influence and aftereffects; because the Rarámuri are shy and private, these occasions also serve as social lubricant between husbands and wives.

## Foodways

The staples are maize, beans, greens, squash and tobacco, with chilli, potatoes, tomatoes and sweet potatoes in more Mexicanized districts. Corn is planted in February and March with oxen, often borrowed since not every household owns one; it flowers in August and is harvested by November, then cooked or stored. The standard corn dishes are *pinole*, tortillas, *atole*, *tamales*, and ears boiled or roasted — and a wide fired-clay bowl, *jícara*, in the collection was used specifically for roasting maize. Beans, essential for protein, are boiled and then fried; beans and tamales are the food carried on journeys. Wheat and fruit — apples, apricots, figs, oranges — came in with the missionaries and remain minor. Meat is less than a twentieth of the diet, mostly fish, chicken and squirrel, with cattle, sheep and goats killed on ceremonial occasions; deer and wild turkey are taken by persistence hunting, followed at a steady pace for a day or two until the animal drops. *Batári* is brewed year-round from sprouted corn — malted, spread in a shallow basket under pine needles and kept moist for four or five days until the starch has turned to sugar, mashed and boiled for eight hours, then combined with a fire-fermented herb paste and left three to four days more. It is drunk soon after, since it can spoil within a day. When corn is scarce the same drink is made from still-green stalks, in which case it is called *paciki*, or from cactus fruit, shrubs, wheat and trees. The dietary researcher William Connors linked the traditional diet to a low incidence of diseases such as Type 2 diabetes; where processed goods have replaced the staples, that advantage is eroding.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used say little about Rarámuri narrative art, and nothing about an epic cycle. What they document is the ceremonial speech register: chanters who lead a community in chants and rhythms through a fiesta, and the sermon delivered to a boy at his first drink. One stylistic convention of Rarámuri storytelling is recorded in linguistic description — narrators sometimes drop the demonstrative before an animal's name, treating the animal as a proper noun and ranking it higher on the animacy scale, and narratives favour an object-verb-subject word order uncommon in ordinary speech. The oldest written document about the people from inside the colonial encounter is the Jesuit report of 1691 on Rarámuri resistance to evangelization, *Historia de la tercera rebelión tarahumara*. Present-day documentation includes a Rarámuri translation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Tarahumara Books project, which publishes work by, for and about the Ralámuli of Chihuahua in Ralámuli, Spanish and English.

## Language & religion

Rarámuri — endonym *Rarámuri* or *Ralámuli ra'ícha*, 'people language' — is Uto-Aztecan, grouped with its closest relative Guarijío. Within the language *rarámuri* refers specifically to men; a woman is *mukí*, and women collectively *omugí* or *igómale*. Specialists disagree on the dialect count: proposals of two (Western and Eastern), four, and five circulate, and the five tentatively recognized by the Mexican government are not those recognized by Ethnologue; the historian Manuel Orozco y Berra listed Varohio, Guazapare, Pachera and Tubar. The language is used in primary schools, local administration, traditional religious practice and local commerce, but only about 1% of speakers read it, against 20% literate in Spanish. Religion is a syncretism worked out largely without outside supervision after the Jesuits were expelled. God, *Riosi*, is identified with the Indigenous *Onoruame*, 'Great Father'; the Virgin Mary with *Iyeruame*, 'Great Mother'; their sons are the *sukristo* and their daughters the *Santi*. The devil, *Riablo*, is not wholly evil but tainted by its links with the *Chabochi*, the non-Rarámuri, and can be appeased or even enlisted. Many practices carry the sense of *konema*, feeding God — returning a little of what he has given. Like other Uto-Aztecan peoples, the Rarámuri venerate peyote.

- Bernard Fontana, *Tarahumara: Where Night is the Day of the Moon*, Northland Press, 1979.
- John G. Kennedy, *Tarahumara of the Sierra Madre: Beer, Ecology and Social Organization*, AHM Publishing, 1978 (republished as *The Tarahumara of the Sierra Madre: Survivors on the Canyon's Edge*, 1996).
- William L. Merrill, *Rarámuri Souls: Knowledge and Social Process in Northern Mexico*, Smithsonian Institution Scholarly Press, 1988.
- Campbell Pennington, *The Tarahumar of Mexico: Their Environment and Material Culture*, University of Utah Press, 1963 — the standard account of the material culture shown here.
- Gabriela Caballero, *A Grammar of Choguita Rarámuri*, Language Science Press, 2022, and her 2008 Berkeley dissertation on Choguita Rarámuri phonology and morphology.

---
title: "Mixtec"
subtitle: "Mexico"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]
---

## Overview

The Mixtecs — *Mixtecos* in Spanish, from the Nahuatl *mixtecah*, "cloud people," and self-named *ñuù savi*, *nayívi savi*, *ñuù davi* or *nayivi davi*, all translatable as "the land of the rain" — are an Indigenous Mesoamerican people of southern Mexico. Their homeland, *La Mixteca* or *Ñuu Dzahui*, covers more than 40,000 km² across western Oaxaca, southern Puebla and eastern Guerrero, including the Costa Chica and La Montaña regions, and is conventionally divided into the mountainous Mixteca Alta (*Ñuu Savi Sukun*), the hot, dry Mixteca Baja (*Ñuu I'ni*) and the humid Mixteca Costa (*Ñuu Andivi*). Roughly 800,000 Mixtec people live in Mexico today, against an estimated 1.5 million before the Spanish conquest, with large communities in California (about 150,000 as of 2011), New York City, Tijuana, San Diego and Tucson. The Mixtec languages form a major branch of the Oto-Manguean family. In folk-culture terms the Mixtecs matter twice over: as the makers of the surviving pictorial codices, and as weavers of shellfish- and cochineal-dyed cloth whose motifs are still catalogued in museum collections.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Brocaded wedding *huipil*** — A three-panel ceremonial *huipil* woven on the backstrap loom from stripes of hand-spun white cotton, lilac cotton dyed with the secretion of shellfish, and *hiladillo*, cochineal-dyed silk in burgundy; the neck opening is edged with purple satin ribbon and a double-headed bird motif is brocaded in four bands running across the stripes.

**Embroidered wedding *huipil*** — A second wedding form in cotton and silk: three panels of handspun white cotton joined by green silk ribbon, with thicker weft threads inserted periodically to raise horizontal bands in the cotton ground. Silk ribbon runs along the side seams and neck opening, the neck is embroidered with animals and flowers in silk thread, and the double-headed bird appears below the neck opening front and back and again on the shoulders.

***Posahuanco*** — The wrap-around skirt, built from three webs of cloth sewn together and woven in horizontal bands of blue, mauve and maroon with some red. Its distinction lies in the dye triad: cotton coloured with indigo and with shellfish dye, and silk with cochineal.

**Warp-patterned wrap cloth** — A cloth of two webs of cream hand-spun cotton carrying seven warp bands of woven decoration in mauve hand-spun cotton and maroon silk, the bands forming repeating geometric, human and animal designs. In the documented example the mauve dye has bled into the base cloth.

***Servilleta* in *coyuche* cotton** — A backstrap-loom cloth of hand-spun naturally brown cotton (*coyuche* in Spanish) with warp stripes alternating brown and white and a twisted warp-thread fringe at both ends.

**Plaited palm basketry** — Lidded baskets plaited from palm fibre, patterned by setting fuchsia-dyed fibre against an undyed ground in zigzag or geometric registers, with the inside of a base sometimes worked wholly in the dyed fibre and the bottom and lid finished with a single thin cross stitch.

**Motif vocabulary.** Double-headed bird (the dominant wedding-*huipil* motif), owl, scorpion, butterfly, deer, fox — including a fox wearing a crown — cats, rabbit, birds, human figures, flowers, horizontal and warp-band geometric registers, and zigzags in dyed palm.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress in the documented material is built from two loom-woven pieces: the *huipil* above and the wrapped *posahuanco* below, both made of narrow webs sewn together rather than cut and tailored. Ceremonial dress is clearly set apart from daily wear — the wedding *huipil* carries brocaded or embroidered double-headed birds, satin or silk ribbon trim at the neck and seams, and the costly dye pair of shellfish purple and cochineal red, materials that signal expense as much as pattern. The ordinary *servilleta*, by contrast, is left in the undyed browns and whites of *coyuche* cotton. A painted pottery figurine shows a woman in a conical skirt wearing a sombrero and carrying a basket over one arm, which is the only indication of headgear in the records used here. For masquerade there is a carved wooden dance-belt in the form of a horse, painted white with a brown saddle blanket trimmed in red, gold and green, fitted with leather ears, a horsehair mane and twisted-cord reins and stirrups, tied to the dancer's waist with fibre cord. The sources used do not describe men's everyday dress, belts or footwear.

### Architecture

The sources describe the Mixtec built environment archaeologically rather than as a living house form. Settlement began with small agricultural villages from about the 16th century BC — the Cruz phase in the Alta, the Pre-Ñudée and Ñudée phases in the Baja, the Charco phase on the coast — and the first substantial towns, Monte Negro and Huamelulpan in the Alta and Cerro de las Minas in the Baja, appear towards the end of the Middle Preclassic. Mixtec urbanism is distinguished from the rest of Mesoamerica by its plan: Cerro de las Minas was laid out around a group of several small plazas rather than a single great one, with the population distributed around them. The hillside was reshaped with terraces called *coo yuu* (lama-bordo), so the city is threaded with stairways, and its walls carried reliefs inscribed in the *ñuiñe* script. During the Classic period the Baja cities — Cerro de las Minas, Diquiyú and others — were fortified, with administrative and religious buildings set on hill slopes and dwellings on ground of easier access. The Mixtecs also built at Monte Albán after taking the city from the Zapotecs, and made major constructions at Tilantongo, Mitla, Cuilapan, Yucuñudahui and Tututepec.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The documented domestic pottery is burnished and slipped, in orange or white, often lightly fired and fire-stained. Standard forms are the water-jug — ovoid or round-bottomed, tapering to a long neck that flares at the lip, with two or three looped handles evenly spaced around the shoulder — the round water-bottle, and the miniature versions of both. Painted wares carry bands of geometric design above animals: scorpions in white on a gourd-shaped double-bellied pot, butterfly, bird and flower across the handles of another, green and red geometric work on white slip. A parallel figural repertoire covers candle-holders modelled as fish, as long-necked four-legged animals with a candle tube on each flank and a smaller animal on the back, and a pottery *candelabrum* built as a tree of life: two tree shapes on four legs, an angel on wire at the base of the trunk, above it a figure with a cross in one hand and a skull in the other, a bird and dog on wire, five candle tubes along the outer edge, and flowers, birds and leaves mounted on wire. Gourds are carved on the outside with geometric fields and animals and fitted with lids tied on by twisted cord. In metal, the Mixtecs were, in West's phrase, "the foremost goldsmiths of Mesoamerica," working by lost-wax casting of gold and its alloys.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Mixtec mastery of jewelry and mosaic, with gold and turquoise prominent, was regarded throughout ancient Mesoamerica, and the output of Mixtec goldsmiths formed an important part of the tribute the Mixtecs paid to the Aztecs. Turquoise mosaic masks carried political and religious weight at once: they were given as gifts to seal political alliances, worn in ceremonies in which the wearer impersonated a god, and fixed to funerary bundles that were treated as oracles. The sources used do not cover tattooing, body paint or hair practice.

## Music & performance

Instruments are thinly documented here: the one object is a rattle made from a round gourd mounted on a wooden dowel, filled with pebbles or seeds, its surface cut away to leave brown designs of two birds, a rabbit and a fox on a beige ground, the handle painted in fuchsia and green stripes. Beyond objects, the sources make one substantial point about Mixtec music, and it concerns transmission rather than repertoire: through the five centuries after the Conquest, when Mixtec literature was confined to the popular sphere, it survived chiefly by oral means — through music and through the conduct of ritual. In the contemporary period, the poem *Yunu Yukuninu* ("Tree, Hill of Yucuninu") by Juan de Dios Ortiz Cruz of the Mixteca Alta was set to music by Lila Downs, named in the sources as one of the leading figures in contemporary Mixtec music. The same writer has collected the lyrical compositions of his region. The sources used do not name Mixtec song genres or ensemble types.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document dance only through one object, the carved wooden horse dance-belt described above, worn at the waist on fibre cords threaded through four holes around its central opening — a horse-mounted masquerade of the kind the catalogue records without naming the dance. No named dance or dramatic tradition appears in the sources used.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not give an annual festival calendar. What they do document is ritual practice attached to places and objects. The Colossal Natural Bridge, a cave site in the Coixtlahuaca Basin, is an important sacred place for the Mixtec; among the *ñuiñe* "colossal heads," small stone sculptures of anthropomorphic heads found in the Baja, some are objects of worship in the Indigenous communities of the Mixteca guerrerense today. In the pre-Hispanic period, turquoise mosaic masks were worn in ceremonies of divine impersonation and attached to oracular funerary bundles. The Classic period saw the consolidation of the cult of rain and lightning in the divinised figure of Dzahui, whose local version appears on Baja urns alongside the Old God of Fire, effigies close in character to the Zapotec Pitao Cocijo. Of life-cycle rites, the one the collection records directly is marriage: the three-panel wedding *huipil*, woven in shellfish purple and cochineal silk and marked with the double-headed bird, is a garment made for that occasion and distinct from everyday cloth. The founding myth of the Arrowman of the Sun ties ritual to the agricultural year, since the people, settled on land won from the Sun, were hastened to plant their corn *milpas* that same night.

## Foodways

The sources treat subsistence rather than cuisine. The economy of the first agricultural settlements in La Mixteca, from around the third millennium BC, rested on the four basic Mesoamerican crops: chili, corn, beans and squash. Corn is also cosmological — in the Mixtec creation account the four creator gods make humanity from corn — and the corn *milpa* is the field the first Mixtecs are said to have planted overnight to hold the land they had won from the Sun. In the colonial period local exchange turned on agricultural commodities and Indigenous crafts, handled regionally in the second half of the period by bilingual Mixtec merchants dealing in both Spanish and Indigenous goods. The vocabulary of newly introduced foods entered the language directly: *limun*, from Spanish *limón*, is recorded in San Martín Duraznos, Oaxaca, where the lemon is also called *tzikua Iya*, "sour orange." The sources used do not describe cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial food or drink traditions.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Mixtec are known in anthropology for their codices, phonetic pictures painted on deerskin in screenfold "fold-book" form. Four survive, narrating the exploits of Lord Eight Deer, named for the day of his birth and surnamed Jaguar Claw, who conquered and united most of the Mixteca: the Codex Bodley, the Codex Zouche-Nuttall and the Codex Vindobonensis in European collections, and the Codex Colombino in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. The genealogical screenfold shown in this atlas records twenty-six generations of a noble family, with subsidiary lines and a commentary in a native Mexican language, on sixteen double-sided leather pages. After the Conquest, codices gave way to *lienzos*, large pictorial cloths glossed in the Latin alphabet, of which the Lienzo Seler II from Coixtlahuaca is the most notable. The key to reading the codices was recovered only in the mid-20th century, largely by Alfonso Caso. The modern revival runs through the Asociación de Escritores en Lenguas Indígenas, founded in 1993, the Casa del Escritor en Lengua Indígena three years later, the Nezahualcóyotl Prize, and writers of the Mixteca Alta such as Raúl Gatica, whose *Asalto a la palabra* gathered work by several Mixtec poets.

## Language & religion

Mixtec belongs to the Mixtecan group of Oto-Manguean and is closely related to Trique and Cuicatec. Its varieties, spoken by over half a million people, form a dialect continuum with abrupt boundaries; depending on the criteria, there are between a dozen and fifty-three Mixtec languages, and SIL International has assigned distinct ISO codes to more than fifty. Speakers call the language *tu'un savi*, *sahan sau*, *dahan davi* and many other local forms, meaning "word of the rain"; Classical Mixtec had *dzaha dzavui*. Tone is central — commonly three levels, with nine in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec — alongside contrastive nasalization and glottalization. The pre-Hispanic pictorial system was supplemented after the Conquest by missionary grammars and a Latin orthography, revised in recent decades by the Academy of the Mixtec Language and the Secretariat of Public Education. The chief pre-Hispanic deity was Dzahui, god of rain and patron of the Mixtec nation, with Nine Wind-Coo Dzahui as the civilising hero who brought agriculture; Roman Catholicism arrived with the missionaries of the 16th century.

## At a glance

| Who | The Mixtec, an Indigenous Mesoamerican people who call themselves 'the people of the rain' |
| Where | Southern Mexico: western Oaxaca, southern Puebla, eastern Guerrero, plus large diaspora communities in California, New York, and other US cities |
| How many | About 800,000 in Mexico today; roughly 150,000 in California as of 2011 |

| Known for | Surviving pictorial codices narrating the exploits of Lord Eight Deer · Shellfish- and cochineal-dyed cloth woven on backstrap looms · Gold and turquoise jewelry and mosaic work · Distinctive multi-plaza settlement patterns · Codex screenfolds recording noble genealogies |

## Overview

The Mixtec are an Indigenous people of southern Mexico whose homeland spans three regions: the mountainous Mixteca Alta, the hot Mixteca Baja, and the humid Mixteca Costa. They are celebrated in anthropology for their surviving pictorial codices painted on deerskin and their mastery of textiles dyed with shellfish purple and cochineal red. Their cities were laid out around multiple small plazas rather than a single grand plaza, and they later built at Monte Albán, Tilantongo, and other major Mesoamerican sites. Today they number about 800,000 in Mexico with significant diaspora communities in the United States.

## Material culture

Mixtec material culture centers on backstrap-loom textiles with costly dyes, refined ceramics, and masterwork in gold and turquoise.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Mixtec weavers created three-panel textiles using hand-spun cotton and silk dyed with shellfish, cochineal, and indigo, featuring woven or brocaded motifs.

- **Brocaded wedding huipil** (*huipil*) — A three-panel ceremonial shirt woven in white cotton, shellfish-dyed lilac, and burgundy cochineal silk, with a double-headed bird brocaded in four bands across the stripes and purple satin trim at the neck.
- **Embroidered wedding huipil** (*huipil*) — A second wedding form with three cotton panels joined by green silk ribbon, thicker weft threads raising horizontal bands, silk embroidered neck with animals and flowers, and double-headed birds on front, back, and shoulders.
- **Wrap-around skirt** (*posahuanco*) — Built from three webs of cloth sewn together in horizontal bands of blue, mauve, and maroon, combining cotton dyed with indigo and shellfish dye with cochineal-dyed silk.
- **Plain brown and white cloth** (*servilleta in coyuche cotton*) — A backstrap-loom cloth of hand-spun naturally brown cotton with warp stripes alternating brown and white and a twisted fringe at both ends.
- **Plaited palm baskets** — Lidded baskets plaited from palm fiber with fuchsia-dyed fiber set against undyed ground in zigzag and geometric patterns, finished with thin cross stitch.

### Clothing & dress

Women's dress consists of two sewn loom-woven pieces: the huipil and wrapped posahuanco, with ceremonial garments distinguished by costly dyes and elaborate trim.

- **Ceremonial wedding huipil** (*huipil*) — Made for marriage ceremonies in shellfish purple and cochineal silk with satin or silk ribbon trim and double-headed bird motifs, marking expense and status.
- **Everyday huipil** (*huipil*) — Plain undyed browns and whites of coyuche cotton, in contrast to the elaborate wedding form.
- **Dance-belt horse** — A carved wooden horse painted white with a brown saddle blanket trimmed in red, gold and green, fitted with leather ears, horsehair mane, and twisted-cord reins and stirrups, tied to the waist for masquerade.

### Architecture

Mixtec cities were laid out around multiple small plazas rather than single great plazas, and hillsides were terraced with stairways to accommodate the population.

- **Cerro de las Minas** — A Baja city built around several small plazas with the population distributed around them, featuring terraced hillsides with stairways and walls inscribed in ñuiñe script.
- **Monte Negro** — One of the first substantial towns in the Mixteca Alta, appearing towards the end of the Middle Preclassic period.
- **Hillside terrace system** (*coo yuu (lama-bordo)*) — Terraces that reshaped hillsides to allow settlement and were threaded with stairways throughout the city.
- **Classic period fortified cities** — Cities in the Baja such as Cerro de las Minas and Diquiyú with administrative and religious buildings on hill slopes and dwellings on lower ground.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Mixtec potters made burnished and slipped wares in orange or white, from water-jugs with geometric and animal designs to elaborate candelabra shaped as trees of life.

- **Water-jug** — Ovoid or round-bottomed vessels tapering to a long flaring neck with two or three looped handles evenly spaced around the shoulder.
- **Painted pottery candelabrum** — A tree-of-life form built on four legs with an angel at the trunk base, a figure holding a cross and skull, birds and dogs on wire, five candle tubes, and flowers and leaves mounted on wire.
- **Carved gourd vessels** — Gourds carved on the outside with geometric fields and animals and fitted with lids tied on by twisted cord.
- **Gold jewelry and ornaments** — Works by the Mixtec, regarded as the foremost goldsmiths of Mesoamerica, created by lost-wax casting of gold and its alloys.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Mixtec jewelers and mosaicists created turquoise mosaic masks and gold work that held political and religious weight throughout ancient Mesoamerica.

- **Turquoise mosaic masks** — Masks given as gifts to seal political alliances, worn in ceremonies impersonating gods, and attached to funerary bundles treated as oracles.
- **Gold jewelry** — Mixtec goldsmiths' output formed an important part of the tribute paid to the Aztecs and was highly valued across Mesoamerica.

## Music & performance

Mixtec music was transmitted orally through five centuries after the Conquest, surviving largely through ritual and community practice.

- **Gourd rattle** — A round gourd mounted on a wooden dowel, filled with pebbles or seeds, its surface cut away to show brown designs of two birds, a rabbit and a fox on a beige ground, with a fuchsia and green striped handle.
- **Contemporary Mixtec music** — The poem 'Yunu Yukuninu' by Juan de Dios Ortiz Cruz was set to music by Lila Downs, one of the leading figures in contemporary Mixtec music.

## Dance & theatre

Dance traditions are documented only through a carved wooden horse dance-belt worn at the waist for masquerade.

- **Horse dance-belt masquerade** — A carved wooden horse worn at the waist on fiber cords, painted white with a brown saddle blanket trimmed in red, gold, and green, with leather ears and horsehair mane.

## Festivals & rituals

Mixtec ritual practice is tied to sacred places and objects, with the most documented life-cycle rite being marriage ceremonies marked by distinctive textiles.

- **Colossal Natural Bridge** — A cave site in the Coixtlahuaca Basin that is an important sacred place for the Mixtec.
- **Colossal head sculptures** (*ñuiñe*) — Small stone sculptures of anthropomorphic heads found in the Baja, some of which are objects of worship in Mixteca guerrerense communities today.
- **Wedding ceremony** — Marked by a three-panel huipil woven in shellfish purple and cochineal silk with double-headed bird motifs, distinct from everyday cloth.
- **Divine impersonation ceremony** — Pre-Hispanic ceremonies in which turquoise mosaic masks were worn by the wearer impersonating a god.

## Foodways

The Mixtec economy rested on four basic Mesoamerican crops: corn, chili, beans, and squash, with corn holding cosmological significance.

- **Corn milpa** (*milpa*) — The field first Mixtecs planted overnight to hold the land won from the Sun; corn is also central to the Mixtec creation account where four gods make humanity from it.
- **Four basic Mesoamerican crops** — Corn, chili, beans, and squash formed the foundation of settlements from around the third millennium BC.
- **Lemon** (*tzikua Iya (sour orange) or limun*) — A newly introduced Spanish crop recorded in San Martín Duraznos, Oaxaca, with both Spanish and indigenous names.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Mixtec are known for their surviving pictorial codices painted on deerskin in screenfold form, narrating the exploits of Lord Eight Deer.

- **Codex Bodley** — One of four surviving codices narrating the exploits of Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, housed in a European collection.
- **Codex Colombino** — A surviving codex narrating the exploits of Lord Eight Deer, held in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City.
- **Genealogical screenfold** — A pictorial record on sixteen double-sided leather pages showing twenty-six generations of a noble family with subsidiary lines and native language commentary.
- **Lienzo Seler II** (*lienzo*) — A post-Conquest pictorial cloth glossed in the Latin alphabet from Coixtlahuaca, representing the transition from codices to lienzos.
- **Modern Mixtec writers** — Writers of the Mixteca Alta such as Raúl Gatica, whose work appears in contemporary collections like 'Asalto a la palabra' gathering Mixtec poets.

## Language & religion

Mixtec belongs to the Oto-Manguean language family and is tone-based; pre-Hispanic worship of Dzahui the rain god was supplemented by Roman Catholicism after the 16th century.

- **Mixtec language** (*tu'un savi (or sahan sau, dahan davi)*) — Over fifty varieties forming a dialect continuum with abrupt boundaries, spoken by over half a million people; means 'word of the rain' in local forms.
- **Tone system** — Commonly three tonal levels, with nine in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec, alongside contrastive nasalization and glottalization.
- **Dzahui** — Chief pre-Hispanic deity, god of rain and patron of the Mixtec nation, whose cult was consolidated during the Classic period.
- **Nine Wind-Coo Dzahui** — The civilising hero who brought agriculture to the Mixtec people.

## Glossary

- *Huipil* — A sleeveless shirt woven on the backstrap loom in three panels
- *Posahuanco* — A wrap-around skirt made from three webs of cloth sewn together
- *Coyuche* — Naturally brown hand-spun cotton
- *Coo yuu* — Hillside terraces (lama-bordo) used to reshape settlement areas
- *Ñuiñe* — Mixtec script used to inscribe reliefs on walls; also refers to colossal head sculptures
- *Milpa* — A field planted with corn and other basic crops
- *Tu'un savi* — Mixtec self-name for the language meaning 'word of the rain'
- *Dzahui* — Pre-Hispanic Mixtec god of rain and nation's patron
- *Lienzo* — A large post-Conquest pictorial cloth glossed in the Latin alphabet
- *Servilleta* — A small backstrap-loom cloth
- *Codex* — A pictorial screenfold narrative painted on deerskin in pre-Hispanic form

## Sources & further reading

- Kevin Terraciano, The Mixtecs of Colonial Oaxaca: Nudzahui History, Sixteenth Through Eighteenth Centuries, Stanford University Press, 2004 (ISBN 978-0804751049)
- Gabina Aurora Pérez Jiménez and Maarten Jansen, The Mixtec Pictorial Manuscripts: Time, Agency and Memory in Ancient Mexico, 2010 (ISBN 978-90-04-19358-1)
- Antonio de los Reyes, Arte en lengua mixteca — the colonial grammar that sets out the six-region division of La Mixteca
- Alfonso Caso, who recovered the reading of the Mixtec codices; Ronald Spores on the states of the Nochixtlán valley; John Paddock, who named the ñuiñe culture of the Mixteca Baja; Barbro Dahlgren on the limits of the Mixtec region

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtec_culture
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtec_language
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixtec_religion
- British Museum online collection (the pottery, textiles, basketry, gourds and genealogical codex shown here): https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection

title: "Tzotzil"
subtitle: "Mexico"
region: "Latin America"
tags: [ethnography, latin-america]

## Overview

The Tzotzil are an Indigenous Maya people of the central highlands of Chiapas in southern Mexico, numbering about 298,000 as of 2000. Their largest municipal populations are Chamula (48,500), San Cristóbal de las Casas (30,700) — known by its Tzotzil name *Jovel*, and still regarded as the cultural capital of Chiapas — and Zinacantán (24,300). Their language belongs to the Tzeltalan sub-branch of the Mayan family, descended from the proto-Ch'ol spoken in the late classic period at sites such as Palenque and Yaxchilan; the name *tzotzil* originally meant "bat people," from *sotz'* "bat," while speakers call the language *Bats'i k'op*, "true language." In folk-culture terms the Tzotzil matter above all for backstrap-loom weaving: the museum holdings shown here are dominated by brocaded and embroidered garments whose patterning is specific to individual highland townships.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Backstrap loom weaving** — Nearly every Tzotzil textile in these collections was woven on a backstrap loom: a tree-anchored twined rope, a series of wooden dowels wrapped with "heading cords," flat tapered battens, and a weaver's strap, or *mecapal*, plaited from vegetable fibre and passed around the weaver's waist. One collected loom was acquired with its weft-brocaded web still in progress, burgundy, yellow and green wool on a white cotton ground. Cloth is woven in narrow webs and seamed; spinning was done with a wooden stick pointed at both ends and a pottery whorl.

**Huipil** — The woman's blouse or long overdress. A Chiapas example is built from three webs of white cotton sewn together, folded and seamed at the sides with a cut rounded neck opening, and brocaded in red geometric patterning with multicoloured accents around the neck and across the shoulders. Commercial cotton thread, *hilaza*, is used alongside handspun yarn.

**Enredo** — The wrap-around skirt, indigo-dyed. A San Andrés Larráinzar skirt is a dark blue plain weave of two narrow webs joined by cross-stitch seams worked on the front face in red, yellow, pink, green and violet wool, with white stripes produced by white weft threads. Another wrap skirt is embroidered in satin stitch with multicoloured acrylic yarn and artificial silk: stripes along the seams, a band of flowers and birds at the hem, two bands of flowers at the top.

**Faja** — The woven sash or belt that holds the *enredo* up. Zinacantán women's belts are warp-faced weaves of red yarn with ornamental green stripes, the warp beginning and ending in loops; Huixtán belts are red with yellow edge borders, described in the catalogue as characteristic of that township. A wool belt woven on the backstrap loom is red with black stripes, with braided fringes knotted together at each end. One woman's waist-sash of coarsely handspun wool is red with a yellow stripe along either edge.

**Woman's cape and cloak** — A cotton cape woven with four selvages is patterned in red and white warp stripes, edged with a narrow multicoloured warp band, and fastened at the neck with two braided cords and tassels. A heavier woman's cloak of wool and orlon carries a blue and light-blue geometric field with orange, blue and fuchsia side borders and ties wrapped in fuchsia, orange, turquoise and green.

**Duk** — The man's square cloth of striped or checked cotton with pink wool tassels at the corners, worn around the neck and over the shoulders at Zinacantán. The same kerchief, blue and white checked with a fuchsia wool tassel in each corner, appears on a miniature man's costume.

**Bolsa** — Small carrying bags. One Larráinzar *bolsa*, handwoven of cotton and embroidered in green, red and orange, was used for carrying money. A bag of factory-made cotton, *manta*, is covered in running-stitch embroidery: bands of red alternating with turquoise, orange, purple, green, violet and yellow stripes forming diamond patterns, gathered with a red drawstring. Shoulder-bags are netted from dyed and undyed maguey fibre with a purple and fuchsia band at the top and a leather strap.

**Motif vocabulary.** Red geometric brocade at neck and shoulder; warp stripes in red and white; bands of flowers and of flowers-with-birds along skirt hems; diamond patterns in embroidered bands; indigo grounds broken by white weft stripes; cross-stitch on seams; zigzag lines on hat crowns; a border of toad-like animals on a baby's bonnet.

### Clothing & dress

Men's dress consists of a shirt, short pants, a neckerchief, a hat and a wool poncho; women wear a blouse or long overdress, the *huipil*, an indigo-dyed *enredo*, a cotton sash and a shawl. The collected hats are of palm or other vegetable fibre: a braided strip coiled and sewn into a wide-brimmed hat with a rounded crown ending in a triangular point, a brown band at the rim and around the top of the crown, and an orange and red zigzag sewn around the crown's centre. A miniature costume shows the festive version of the same hat — slats forming a pointed crown, a dark fibre band, and ribbons in yellow, pink, violet, green, white, fuchsia, blue and yellow sewn to the top and sides — worn with a red and white striped *cotón* fringed at both ends. Infants were dressed in gathered white cotton bonnets with a self-fabric fringe and dense multicoloured embroidery on a red base. The sources used here do not describe footwear.

### Architecture

Houses were traditionally built of wattle and daub or of lumber, usually with thatched roofs. Beyond that, the sources used for this profile say nothing about Tzotzil house form, interior arrangement or architectural decoration; what they do record is that the built environment is religiously charged rather than ornamented — ceremonial circuits are walked counterclockwise around the four corners of houses and fields and end at the centre, and the ceremonial centre of a settlement holds the "navel," a mound of earth at the middle of a world conceived as a square. Any Tzotzil who takes mud for house walls or limestone for lime is held to owe the Earth Lord, who owns all land and its resources, compensation in a ceremony.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The most distinctive Tzotzil pottery form in these collections is the *incensario*, a pottery incense burner on a circular base that tapers to a cylindrical stem and flares out into a bowl, with three sets of three prongs on the rim; examples survive with an orange slip, with a beige slip, and plainly fire-stained, one with its lower half painted orange and the bowl striped and dotted. Spinning equipment — a double-pointed wooden spindle with a pottery whorl — and the wooden backstrap loom with its plaited *mecapal* are the other recurring household objects. Figurative work includes a pottery figure wearing a glazed pottery sombrero, a blue cloth tunic and a red plastic sash, and dolls made from maize leaves with cloth heads and braided corn-silk hair tied with red and yellow yarn. The sources record no Tzotzil metalwork.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used here do not cover Tzotzil jewelry or body adornment; the only hair practice they document is indirect — figures made for nativity scenes are given black wool hair braided and decorated with fuchsia, blue and yellow wool.

## Music & performance

Musical documentation in these sources is slight but concrete. A Tzotzil guitar carved from a single hourglass-shaped wooden body, with a central soundhole, a glued-on bridge and neck, wooden frets, twelve wooden tuning pegs and twelve metal strings, carries two leather loops — one on the body, one on the neck — for a strap, so it was played standing and in procession. The language itself preserves a word for flute, *'ama*. Recordings of Tzotzil made between 1964 and 1972 for Victoria Bricker's Mayan Languages Collection, now at the Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America, include elicited humorous narratives, songs and prayers, as well as live recordings of ritual humor at the fiestas of Saint Lawrence, Christmas, New Year's Day, Epiphany and Saint Sebastian — which places song and prayer firmly inside the festival cycle rather than on a concert stage. Tzotzil-language programming is broadcast today by the CDI radio stations XEVFS, from Las Margaritas, and XECOPA, at Copainalá. The sources name no Tzotzil ensemble type or song genre beyond this.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used for this profile do not describe named Tzotzil dances or dramatic forms; the nearest documented performance genre is the ritual humor recorded at the township fiestas of Saint Lawrence, Saint Sebastian, Christmas, New Year's Day and Epiphany, and the nativity scene, or *nacimiento*, built as a tableau of maize-leaf figures mounted on wooden pegs — a kneeling shepherd with a painted face and an apron over shirt and trousers, and a cowled Wise Man in a dark robe with a red wool sash, holding a nut shell in both hands as his offering.

## Festivals & rituals

The documented festival calendar is the Catholic one as kept in Tzotzil townships: Saint Sebastian, Epiphany, New Year's Day, Christmas and the fiesta of Saint Lawrence, each an occasion for prayer, song and licensed ritual joking. Carved wooden or plaster images and pictures of Catholic saints are revered, dressed in a mixture of colonial and Zinacanteco-style clothing. Alongside this runs a body of ritual that is not Catholic in origin. Priests walk ceremonial circuits counterclockwise around the four corners of houses and fields, ending at the centre with offerings. Anyone drawing on water holes, trees, mud or limestone owes a compensating ceremony to the Earth Lord, pictured in modern times as a large, fat, rich Ladino living underground. The inner soul, *ch'ulel*, is composed of thirteen parts, and a person who loses one or more needs a curing ceremony performed by a shaman to recover them — soul loss being caused by the fright of a fall or of seeing a demon at night, by punishment from the ancestral gods, or by witchcraft that sells the soul to the Earth Lord. The second soul, the *wayhel*, is shared with a wild animal companion, the *chanul* — jaguars, ocelots, coyotes, squirrels, opossums — penned by the ancestral gods in four corrals inside the Senior Large Mountain in the east; if a *chanul* is released, its person is in mortal danger until a long ceremony rounds the animal up and returns it. At death the inner soul goes to *Katibak*, the world of the dead at the centre of the earth, and relives its life in reverse before being assigned to a newborn of the opposite sex; baptized infants and women who die in childbirth go instead to *Winajel*, in the Sun.

## Foodways

The sources used for this profile do not describe Tzotzil cooking, dishes or drink. What they document is production and trade: the Tzotzil made salt from wells near Ixtapa and traded it throughout the Chiapas highlands both before and after the Spanish Conquest, and just before the Conquest they exported quetzal feathers and amber to the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán. Maize is present in the collections only as a material — the leaves of the plant are the body of dolls and of nativity figures, and corn silk their hair.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tzotzil narrative, as these sources preserve it, is cosmological. The god Manojel-Tojel created human beings by leading them out of the caves of the original hills, and each patron god then "installed himself in a hill, by order of the gods of the four corners of the earth," so that every town has its sacred mountain. Yahwal Balamil lives inside the earth, rides a deer with serpent bridles, releases the water-filled clouds through caves, and announces himself with the croaking of frogs. The ancestral couples, the *Totilme'il* or "Fathers–Mothers," inhabit local hills and are the most important gods; the world rests on the shoulders of the *Vashak*. A Spanish chronicler recorded that the ancestors of Zinacantán "discovered a stone bat and considered it God and worshiped it." Spoken genres were documented on tape between 1964 and 1972: humorous narratives, songs, prayers, and didactic lessons and texts. Written resources begin with Otto Stoll's word-lists in *Zur Ethnographie der Republik Guatemala* (1884) and run through the Smithsonian Institution's 1975 dictionary of some 30,000 Tzotzil–English entries to the INALI writing norm of 2011 and a Tzotzil New Testament.

## Language & religion

Tzotzil is a Mayan language of the Tzeltalan sub-branch, most closely related to Tzeltal; with Tzeltal and Ch'ol it is among the most widely spoken languages of Chiapas after Spanish, and many speakers are monolingual. Six dialects are named for their regions: Chamula, Zinacantán, San Andrés Larráinzar, Huixtán, Chenalhó and Venustiano Carranza. Word order is verb–object–subject and agreement is ergative–absolutive; counted nouns take numeral classifiers matched to the shape of the thing counted. Some primary schools and a secondary school in central Chiapas teach in Tzotzil. Religion is syncretic: under Catholic influence the Sun, "Our Father Heat," has been identified with God the Father or Jesus Christ and the Moon, "Our Holy Mother," with the Virgin Mary, while Venus is "Sweeper of the Path" because it precedes the Sun. In 2013 Pope Francis approved Tzotzil translations of the prayers for Mass and the sacraments.

## Sources & further reading

- Laughlin, Robert M. *Beware the Great Horned Serpent!: Chiapas Under the Threat of Napoleon*. IMS Studies on Culture and Society, no. 8. Albany: Institute of Mesoamerican Studies, University at Albany, SUNY, 2003.
- López Austin, Alfredo, and Leonardo López Luján. *Mexico's Indigenous Past*. Translated by Bernard R. Ortiz de Montellano. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 2001.
- Díaz López, Óscar, et al. *Smelolal stsʼibael batsʼi kʼop tsotsil / Norma de escritura de la lengua tsotsil*. Mexico City: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI), 2011.
- Stoll, Otto. *Zur Ethnographie der Republik Guatemala*, 1884 — the earliest substantial Tzotzil word-lists and grammar.
- Documentation projects: Victoria Bricker's Mayan Languages Collection at the Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America (Tzotzil recordings, 1964–1972); the Smithsonian Institution's Tzotzil dictionary (1975); Heriberto Avelino's 2009 work on the disputed tone contrast in the Venustiano Carranza variety, following Sarles (1966).
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzotzil
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tzotzil_language
- Smithsonian Folkways search: https://folkways.si.edu/search?query=Tzotzil
- British Museum collection online: https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection (source of the *huipil*, wrap skirt, cloak, cape, sashes, hats, *incensarios*, backstrap loom, guitar and maize-leaf figures shown here)
